analysis.research_question_and_background: Respiratory viral infections, particularly Influenza A and SARS‐CoV‐2, remain major public health concerns in endemic settings such as Pakistan, where high influenza‐like illness burden and limited genomic data underscore the need for surveillance to guide vaccine strategies.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This study assessed respiratory virus circulation and genetic diversity among ILI cases at a secondary‐care hospital in Islamabad during the 2025–2026 winter season.
analysis.methods: Among 170 qRT‐PCR‐tested cases, Influenza A was detected in 24.1%, SARS‐CoV‐2 in 1.17%, and Influenza B was not detected. Whole‐genome sequencing of 21 Influenza A(H3N2) isolates revealed co‐circulation of subclade K (52.4%), J.2.2 (28.6%), and J.2 (9.5%).
analysis.main_results: Influenza A positivity was slightly higher in females (25.0%), with highest burden in individuals aged 11–20 years. Phylogenetic analysis showed subclade K clustering with recent isolates from North America, Oceania, Europe, and WHO‐recommended 2026–2027 Northern Hemisphere H3N2 vaccine strains, whereas J.2 and J.2.2 aligned with earlier vaccine‐like strains. NA analysis showed predominance of clade B.4.2.2 associated with K‐lineage and relatedness to recent North American strains. Subclade K exhibited conserved HA substitutions (K2N, S144N, N158D, I160K, Q173R, T328A) and HA2 S49N with limited variation. No antiviral resistance mutations were detected.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Overall, findings demonstrate predominance and genetic stability of H3N2 subclade K and support continuous genomic surveillance for vaccine strain selection and influenza preparedness.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform vaccine strain selection by showing subclade K's alignment with WHO‐recommended strains and highlight the importance of genomic surveillance in influenza preparedness.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study was conducted at a single secondary‐care hospital, limiting generalizability. However, the evidence strength is high due to comprehensive genomic analysis and direct detection methods.

analysis.summary_en: This study conducted molecular surveillance of Influenza A(H3N2) viruses in Pakistan during the 2025–2026 winter season. Among 170 ILI cases, 24.1% tested positive for Influenza A, with no Influenza B detected. Whole-genome sequencing of 21 H3N2 isolates revealed co-circulation of subclade K (52.4%), J.2.2 (28.6%), and J.2 (9.5%). Subclade K clustered with recent global isolates and WHO-recommended vaccine strains, showing conserved HA substitutions and no antiviral resistance. The findings highlight the predominance of genetically stable subclade K and emphasize the need for continuous genomic surveillance to guide vaccine strategies and influenza preparedness.

analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The key conclusion is that strengthened veterinary surveillance under a One Health framework can improve the detection of viral reassortment events, enhance traceability of viral spread, and support timely risk assessment in intensive livestock systems. The integration of whole-genome sequencing, serological surveillance, and AI technologies under One Health has improved detection of reassortment events and viral traceability. The findings offer a practical, replicable model for other countries to enhance pandemic preparedness by overcoming surveillance fragmentation and fostering cross-sector coordination.

analysis.scope_and_question: This review evaluates seasonal influenza vaccine effectiveness (VE) against A(H1N1)pdm09, A(H3N2), influenza B, and B/Victoria in the Northern Hemisphere, comparing pre- (2010/11-2019/20) and post- (2022/23-2024/25) COVID-19 pandemic periods across three age groups (6 months-17 years, 18-64 years, ≥65 years).
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: A systematic meta-analysis of 85 published test-negative design (TND) studies was conducted. Pooled VE estimates were calculated using inverse-variance random-effects meta-analysis, with heterogeneity quantified by I2 and statistical differences tested by χ2.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Post-pandemic VE against A(H3N2) and influenza B was significantly higher in 6-month-17-year-olds and 18-64-year-olds compared to pre-pandemic. Conversely, VE against A(H1N1)pdm09 was lower post-pandemic in 18-64-year-olds. No significant differences were observed for ≥65-year-olds, and B/Victoria data were limited.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The authors note that factors other than population immunity may explain the observed VE changes. Data for B/Victoria were limited, and no significant differences were found in the ≥65-year-old group, leaving gaps in understanding age-specific VE dynamics.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Further research is needed to explore factors beyond population immunity influencing post-pandemic VE, particularly in older adults and for B/Victoria. Surveillance should continue to monitor VE trends across age groups and virus subtypes.

analysis.summary_en: This systematic meta-analysis compared seasonal influenza vaccine effectiveness (VE) before and after the COVID-19 pandemic using 85 test-negative design studies. Post-pandemic VE against A(H3N2) and influenza B was significantly higher in children and adults, while VE against A(H1N1)pdm09 decreased in adults. No significant changes were observed in older adults, and B/Victoria data were limited. The authors suggest factors beyond population immunity may explain these findings, highlighting the need for further research on VE determinants and continued surveillance across age groups and subtypes.

analysis.study_design_and_population: A multicenter, retrospective test-negative design (TND) was adopted in this study, which enrolled all or a systematic sample of patients aged ≥ 60 years presenting with influenza-like illness (ILI) at designated sentinel hospitals in six cities of Zhejiang Province from October 2024 to July 2025.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated the effectiveness of the seasonal influenza vaccine against the dominant A(H1N1)pdm09 virus in adults aged ≥ 60 years in Zhejiang, China, during the 2024–2025 influenza season. Using a multicenter, retrospective test-negative design, the researchers enrolled patients with influenza-like illness (ILI) and collected epidemiological data and respiratory specimens. They found that 33.81% of enrolled patients were influenza-positive, with A(H1N1)pdm09 being the most prevalent subtype. The overall vaccine effectiveness (VE) was 53.3% (95% CI: 45.4–60.2), with varying effectiveness across age groups. VE decreased over time, from 58.0% within 59 days post-vaccination to 42.8% between 60 and 180 days. The study highlights the moderate protection provided by the vaccine against A(H1N1)pdm09 in the elderly, suggesting that consecutive vaccination may help maintain effectiveness. These findings have implications for public health strategies, particularly in optimizing vaccination schedules for this vulnerable population.

analysis.study_design_and_population: The researchers developed a global transmission model for the two influenza B lineages (B/Yamagata and B/Victoria) and simulated the impacts of pandemic-related contact reductions to explain their divergent outcomes.
analysis.methods: The study used mechanistic transmission modeling combined with worldwide influenza surveillance data, implementing a transient reduction in contacts to mimic pandemic effects and identify parameter values that recapitulated pre-pandemic coexistence and post-pandemic outcomes.
analysis.main_results: The results indicate that B/Yamagata's extinction was mainly driven by its lower basic reproduction number, making it particularly vulnerable during the early phase of the pandemic, while B/Victoria narrowly avoided extinction during the same period.

analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings inform influenza eradication efforts and biosafety policy, including assessing the feasibility of B/Victoria eradication through vaccination and the potential for B/Yamagata's re-emergence if reintroduced.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence strength is moderate, as the study relies on model simulations and surveillance data, which may not capture all real-world complexities, though the model successfully recapitulated observed outcomes.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the apparent global extinction of influenza B/Yamagata after the COVID-19 pandemic. The researchers developed a global transmission model for the two influenza B lineages and simulated pandemic-related contact reductions. Their findings indicate that B/Yamagata's lower basic reproduction number made it particularly vulnerable during the pandemic's early phase, while B/Victoria narrowly avoided extinction. The study concludes that differences in cross-immunity and immune escape were insufficient to explain the outcome, with lower intrinsic transmissibility being the primary factor. These results inform influenza eradication efforts and biosafety policy, including the feasibility of B/Victoria eradication and the potential for B/Yamagata's re-emergence if reintroduced.

analysis.summary_en: This study analyzed the epidemiological characteristics of childhood influenza A virus infections in Hebei, China, from 2020 to 2024. It found that the detection rate of influenza A virus was 20.39% among 298,810 specimens collected from hospitalized children. The infection rate peaked in winter at 29.04% and was lowest in spring and summer at 5.4%. These findings highlight the seasonal variation and high co-infection rate of influenza A virus in children, suggesting the need for enhanced surveillance and protective measures during winter and for children aged 1–5 years. The study's retrospective design and potential for selection bias are limitations, but the large sample size and statistically significant results support a high confidence assessment.

By combining genomic, phylogenetic, and functional data in an intuitive interface, the tool lowers barriers for both specialists and non-specialists in influenza sequence interpretation.

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to investigate influenza infection in patients with hematologic malignancies and identify the risk factors associated with mortality. Cancer patients, especially those with hematologic malignancies, are considered among the most vulnerable groups at risk for severe outcomes from influenza infection.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This cross-sectional descriptive observational study included 90 patients with confirmed influenza infection and hematologic malignancies. analysis.methods: Methods involved collecting data on demographic information, cancer type and status, influenza type, symptoms, laboratory and radiologic findings, length of hospital stay, ICU admissions, and mortality rate from 90 patients with confirmed influenza infection and hematologic malignancies.
analysis.main_results: The mean age of patients was 34.3 ± 26.7 years (median 34, range 2–91). Nearly half (49.3%) were in the maintenance phase of treatment, and 80% were infected with influenza A. analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform surveillance and risk assessment strategies for influenza in hematologic malignancy patients, highlighting the importance of monitoring for comorbidities, LRTIs, and specific malignancies such as MM and AML.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its observational design and the need for validation in larger studies. The age-adjusted analysis identified MM, LRTIs, and comorbidities as potential strong predictors of mortality, but the evidence strength is moderate due to the study's design and sample size.

analysis.summary_en: This cross-sectional observational study investigated influenza infection in patients with hematologic malignancies to identify risk factors for mortality. The study included 90 patients with confirmed influenza infection and HMs, collecting data on demographics, cancer type, influenza type, symptoms, and clinical outcomes. Results showed that ICU admission was significantly linked to older age, comorbidities, lower respiratory tract infections, and certain malignancies like MM, CML, and AML. Higher mortality was observed in patients with MM, AML, comorbidities, and LRTIs. The study concluded that MM, LRTIs, and comorbidities are strong predictors of mortality in this population. While the findings are relevant for understanding influenza outcomes in cancer patients, the study's observational design and small sample size limit the strength of the evidence, necessitating further research.

Functional analyses confirmed that overexpression of ckATP1A1-AS1 restricts infection by multiple IAV subtypes, while its knockdown enhances viral replication. These findings provide strong mechanistic evidence for a novel host defense mechanism against influenza A viruses.

analysis.scope_and_question: Seasonal influenza viruses (A(H1N1)pdm09, A(H3N2), B/Victoria, and historical B/Yamagata) cause approximately one billion infections and up to 650,000 respiratory deaths annually. The central question is how to expand therapeutic strategies beyond current limitations.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: This review critically evaluates the antiviral landscape, focusing on next-generation cap-dependent endonuclease inhibitors (CENIs), resistance implications across all approved drug classes, translational barriers in host-directed therapies and biologics, and H5N1 pandemic preparedness.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Scaffold-level optimization (e.g., Suraxavir marboxil, ZX-7101A, onradivir) can reduce resistance emergence rates. However, all approved classes share a failure pattern: single-target dependence, low-fitness-cost resistance mutations, and a therapeutic window most patients do not reach. Combination therapy shows promise for resistance prevention, but virological benefit does not consistently translate to clinical outcomes in hospitalized patients.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: Host-directed therapies and biologics face translational obstacles: their biological window of activity precedes clinical presentation, and systemic biologics cannot achieve inhibitory concentrations at the respiratory mucosal surface. For H5N1, preparedness relies on a single observationally supported drug class; baloxavir is absent from most stockpiles, and no randomized trial data exists for any antiviral in human H5N1 infection.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Adaptive trial infrastructure, diversified stockpiling to include next-generation CENIs, and equitable global antiviral access are the most urgent priorities in influenza therapeutics.

analysis.summary_en: This review evaluates therapeutic strategies against seasonal influenza, highlighting limitations of current antivirals, including time-dependent efficacy, low resistance barriers, and evidence gaps in high-risk populations. It examines next-generation CENIs, resistance patterns, and translational challenges for host-directed therapies. Key findings include scaffold-level optimization reducing resistance emergence and combination therapy's promise without consistent clinical benefit. Urgent priorities include adaptive trials, diversified stockpiling, and global access to next-generation antivirals, with critical gaps in H5N1 preparedness.

analysis.research_question_and_background: In Japan, seasonal influenza vaccination is recommended for older adults between October and mid-December; however, the optimal vaccination timing remains unclear owing to waning immunity and variable epidemic patterns. In this study, we aimed to assess the effectiveness of different vaccination strategies in reducing influenza-related outcomes in older adults.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Using data from the VENUS Study, we conducted a target trial emulation including adults aged ≥65 years across four influenza seasons (2016/2017, 2017/2018, 2018/2019, and 2019/2020). Outcomes included influenza, influenza-related hospitalization, and all-cause mortality.
analysis.methods: We applied a cloning, censoring, and weighting approach. Each individual was cloned and assigned to one of seven vaccination strategies at the start of October: no vaccination, vaccination during October, October-November, October-December, November, November-December, or December. Risk ratios (RRs) and risk differences (RDs), relative to no vaccination, were estimated at the end of March for each season based on standardized cumulative incidence.
analysis.main_results: Annual cohorts included 131,178-138,438 individuals (median age: 76-78 years; male sex: 40.1-41.0%). The influenza incidences and RRs varied by season. Delayed vaccination was associated with the lowest influenza incidence in 2017/2018 and 2018/2019, but not in the other seasons. Influenza-related hospitalizations showed seasonal trends similar to those of influenza. In contrast, early vaccination strategies generally led to reduced all-cause mortality across all seasons. The RRs were 0.80-0.93, 0.80-0.95, 0.82-1.00, and 0.81-0.96 in the 2016/2017, 2017/2018, 2018/2019, and 2019/2020 seasons, respectively. The RDs were larger for mortality than for the influenza-related outcomes.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The effectiveness of each timing strategy varied depending on the outcome and season. Although delayed vaccination was associated with a lower influenza incidence in some seasons, early vaccination generally reduced all-cause mortality.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that vaccination timing should be tailored to the season and outcome, with early vaccination potentially reducing mortality despite variable effects on influenza incidence. This could inform public health recommendations for optimizing influenza vaccination strategies in older adults.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study used target trial emulation, which may introduce limitations inherent to observational data. However, the large sample size and consistent results across multiple seasons provide moderate confidence in the findings.

analysis.summary_en: This study assessed the optimal timing for influenza vaccination in older adults in Japan using data from the VENUS Study across four seasons. Researchers evaluated seven vaccination strategies, including no vaccination, and measured outcomes such as influenza incidence, hospitalization, and mortality. Results showed that delayed vaccination reduced influenza incidence in some seasons, but early vaccination consistently lowered all-cause mortality across all seasons. The effectiveness varied by season and outcome, with risk ratios for mortality ranging from 0.80 to 1.00. The findings suggest that vaccination timing should be tailored to the season and outcome, with early vaccination potentially offering mortality benefits despite variable effects on influenza incidence.

analysis.study_design_and_population: A PRISMA-guided scoping review of the MEDLINE database was conducted through 31 May 2026, analyzing 83 adult cases reported between 1958 and 2026.
analysis.methods: Published adult cases of influenza-associated encephalopathy, encephalitis, and acute necrotizing encephalopathy were identified and analyzed for demographic characteristics, clinical presentation, neuroimaging findings, treatment, and outcomes.
analysis.main_results: Eighty-three adult cases were included, with a mean age of 45.6 ± 17.8 years, 57.8% male, and two-thirds without underlying comorbidities; neurological symptoms developed a mean of 4.6 days after influenza onset, with influenza A accounting for 80.7% of infections.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that these complications are rare in adults but associated with substantial morbidity and mortality, and this review represents the largest adult cohort reported to date, providing important insights into the clinical spectrum, neurodiagnostic findings, and outcomes.

analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence strength is moderate due to the scoping review design, which relies on case reports and small case series, limiting generalizability and introducing potential biases.

analysis.summary_en: This scoping review analyzed 83 adult cases of influenza-associated encephalopathy, encephalitis, and acute necrotizing encephalopathy reported between 1958 and 2026. The mean age was 45.6 years, with 57.8% male and two-thirds without comorbidities. Neurological symptoms appeared 4.6 days post-influenza onset, with influenza A accounting for 80.7% of cases. Common manifestations included fever (91.6%), altered mental status (86.7%), and seizures (36.1%). Encephalitis was the predominant presentation (44.5%), followed by encephalopathy (31.3%) and ANE (24.1%). MRI frequently showed cerebral hemispheric lesions (53.0%) and bilateral thalamic involvement (36.4%), with EEG abnormalities in 69.6% of patients. Overall mortality was 22.9%, highest in ANE (45.0%), and 28.9% of survivors had persistent neurological sequelae. This review represents the largest adult cohort to date, highlighting substantial morbidity and mortality and the need for collaborative studies to improve diagnosis and treatment.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Acute bronchiolitis is the leading cause of infant hospitalization worldwide, with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) historically predominating. Prospective virological data for the 2025–2026 epidemic season in Morocco were lacking.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A prospective observational cohort study was conducted at the Department of Pediatric Infectious Diseases and Clinical Immunology, Casablanca Mother-Child Hospital, from August 2025 through March 2026. Consecutive infants aged 1–24 months hospitalized with acute viral bronchiolitis underwent nasopharyngeal sampling and multiplex rapid antigen testing for RSV, influenza A, influenza B, and SARS-CoV-2.
analysis.methods: A total of 131 infants were enrolled (median age 4.8 months; male-to-female ratio 0.84:1). At least one virus was identified in 63 patients (48.1%; 95% CI 39.1–57.3%).
analysis.main_results: RSV predominated: 49 sole infections and 2 co-infections with influenza A, totaling 51 positives (80.9% of virus-positive cases; 38.9% of the cohort). Influenza A totaled 8 cases (12.7%), including the 2 co-infections; influenza B accounted for 2 further cases (3.2%). SARS-CoV-2 was not detected.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study provides updated virological data on acute bronchiolitis in Moroccan infants, confirming RSV as the predominant pathogen while also identifying influenza A and B as significant contributors. The findings highlight the need for targeted preventive measures in this population.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: All detected pathogens have licensed preventive options, supporting the introduction of nirsevimab, maternal RSV vaccination, and seasonal influenza vaccination as public health priorities in Morocco. This data can inform local vaccination strategies and surveillance programs.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study was limited to a single center and used rapid antigen testing, which may have reduced sensitivity for some viruses. Despite these limitations, the prospective design and comprehensive testing provide moderate evidence for the local epidemiology of bronchiolitis viruses.

analysis.summary_en: This prospective observational study conducted in Casablanca, Morocco from August 2025 to March 2026 investigated the viral etiology of acute bronchiolitis in hospitalized infants aged 1-24 months. Among 131 enrolled infants, 63 (48.1%) tested positive for at least one virus, with RSV predominating at 51 cases (38.9% of cohort, 80.9% of positives). Influenza A was detected in 8 cases (12.7%) and influenza B in 2 cases (3.2%), while SARS-CoV-2 was not found. The epidemic peaked in January 2026. The authors recommend implementing preventive measures including nirsevimab, maternal RSV vaccination, and seasonal influenza vaccination as public health priorities in Morocco.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Simultaneous detection of influenza A virus (IAV), influenza B virus (IBV), and severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) is essential for rapid differential diagnosis in febrile patients, particularly in the context of co-circulating respiratory viruses.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study aimed to develop a multicolor latex-based immunochromatographic strip as a rapid, sensitive, and reliable tool for analyte detection. analysis.methods: The analytical and clinical performance of the assay were systematically evaluated.
analysis.main_results: The assay enabled detection within 15 minutes, with a limit of detection (LOD) of 102 TCID50/mL for all three viruses. Clinical evaluation showed a sensitivity of 97.73% (215/220) and specificity of 100% (200/200) for SARS-CoV-2 detection, with an overall concordance rate of 98.81% (415/420) and a Kappa value of 0.9762 (p < 0.05), indicating excellent agreement with reference methods.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: This multicolor latex-based immunochromatographic strip exhibits rapid, sensitive, and reliable performance for analyte detection without requiring specialized training.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: It shows strong potential for home self-testing and early screening in settings where SARS-CoV-2 and influenza co-circulate.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The supplied evidence does not report limitations related to the study design or sample size.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to develop a multicolor latex-based immunochromatographic strip for the rapid and simultaneous detection of SARS-CoV-2, influenza A virus (IAV), and influenza B virus (IBV). Clinical results showed high sensitivity (97.73%) and specificity (100%) for SARS-CoV-2, with an overall concordance rate of 98.81% and a Kappa value of 0.9762, indicating strong agreement with reference methods. The assay is reliable, does not require specialized training, and has potential for home self-testing and early screening in co-circulating virus settings. The evidence is limited to abstract-only data, and no specific limitations are reported.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Accurate prediction of antigenic distance between influenza A/H3N2 strains is essential for timely vaccine strain selection, yet traditional hemagglutination inhibition (HI) assays are labour-intensive and limited in throughput.
analysis.study_design_and_population: We present FluQRC, a hybrid Quantum-Classical Reservoir Computing framework for sequence-based antigenic distance prediction.
analysis.methods: On two datasets spanning 1963-2002 (271 strains, 73,441 pairs) and 2003-2025 (888 strains, 788,544 pairs), FluQRC is competitive with four established baselines on the historical set and outperforms all of them on the larger, more challenging 2003-2025 set.
analysis.main_results: FluQRC attains MAE = 0.369, RMSE = 0.635, and R 2 = 0.900 on the 2003-2025 set, a 20.3% reduction in MAE and 14.3% reduction in RMSE over the strongest baseline, raising R 2 from 0.862 to 0.900.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: These results demonstrate the scalability and effectiveness of FluQRC for large-scale antigenic distance prediction.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that FluQRC could improve the efficiency and accuracy of influenza vaccine strain selection by providing a faster, high-throughput alternative to traditional assays.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is based on abstract-only evidence, and while the results are promising, further validation with additional datasets and real-world applications is needed to confirm robustness.

analysis.summary_en: This study introduces FluQRC, a hybrid Quantum-Classical Reservoir Computing framework for predicting antigenic distance between influenza A/H3N2 strains. Tested on two datasets (1963-2002 and 2003-2025), FluQRC outperformed established baselines on the larger dataset, achieving MAE = 0.369, RMSE = 0.635, and R2 = 0.900—a 20.3% reduction in MAE and 14.3% reduction in RMSE over the strongest baseline. The results demonstrate FluQRC's scalability and effectiveness for large-scale antigenic distance prediction, offering a potential high-throughput alternative to traditional labor-intensive assays like hemagglutination inhibition. While promising, further validation is needed to confirm robustness in real-world applications.

The central question is how lactylation influences influenza A virus (IAV) replication, antiviral immunity, and immune evasion.

IAV downregulates SIRT1 expression to counteract this antiviral defense. Lactylation also modulates cGAS-STING, RLR-MAVS, and IFN signaling pathways.

analysis.summary_en: This review explores lactylation as a critical host-virus interaction mechanism in seasonal influenza A and B virus infections. It identifies that lactylation of viral components enhances replication, while host SIRT1-mediated delactylation suppresses infection; however, IAV evades this defense by downregulating SIRT1. Lactylation also modulates key antiviral pathways, including cGAS-STING, RLR-MAVS, and IFN signaling. The review highlights the therapeutic potential of targeting lactate metabolism and SIRT1 but underscores unresolved mechanistic gaps and the need for further research to translate these findings into antiviral strategies.

analysis.research_question_and_background: A multicomponent vaccine targeting seasonal influenza and COVID-19 may reduce disease burden by providing simultaneous protection in a single injection.
analysis.study_design_and_population: We report findings from Part 1 (Japan) of a phase 3, Asia-Pacific, randomized, observer-blind study evaluating immunogenicity, reactogenicity, and safety of mRNA-based multicomponent vaccine mRNA-1083, combining influenza and SARS-CoV-2 antigens. Participants aged ≥50 years were randomized (1:1) to receive mRNA-1083 + placebo or Japan-licensed influenza hemagglutinin (HA) vaccine + mRNA-1273. Overall, 2022 participants were randomized, and 2013 received study intervention.
analysis.methods: The study evaluated immunogenicity, reactogenicity, and safety of mRNA-1083, combining influenza and SARS-CoV-2 antigens, in adults aged ≥50 years in Japan.
analysis.main_results: At Day 29, mRNA-1083 elicited noninferior immune responses versus active comparators for all evaluated influenza strains and SARS-CoV-2. Among high-risk participants, noninferiority was demonstrated for comparator-matched influenza strains and SARS-CoV-2. In the overall study population, mRNA-1083 demonstrated superiority for the comparator-matched influenza strains and for SARS-CoV-2.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that mRNA-1083 elicited noninferior and superior immune responses against influenza and SARS-CoV-2 in the high-risk and overall study population, respectively, with immune responses maintained through 6 months post-vaccination.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings support mRNA-1083 as a single-dose approach to seasonal vaccination against influenza and SARS-CoV-2 in adults ≥50 years, potentially reducing disease burden through simultaneous protection.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study was a phase 3, randomized, observer-blind trial with a large sample size (2013 participants), providing high confidence in the results due to the robust design and comprehensive evaluation of immunogenicity and safety.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated the immunogenicity, reactogenicity, and safety of mRNA-1083, a multicomponent vaccine targeting seasonal influenza and SARS-CoV-2, in adults aged ≥50 years in Japan. The phase 3, randomized, observer-blind trial found that mRNA-1083 elicited noninferior immune responses versus active comparators for all evaluated influenza strains and SARS-CoV-2 at Day 29, with superiority demonstrated in the overall population. Immune responses remained above baseline at Day 181. The vaccine demonstrated an acceptable safety profile, with most adverse reactions being mild to moderate and no cases of myocarditis, pericarditis, or serious adverse events related to the intervention. These findings support mRNA-1083 as a single-dose approach for seasonal vaccination against both influenza and SARS-CoV-2 in older adults.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Respiratory viral infections, particularly Influenza A and SARS-CoV-2, remain major public health concerns in endemic settings such as Pakistan, where high influenza-like illness burden and limited genomic data underscore the need for surveillance to guide vaccine strategies.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This study assessed respiratory virus circulation and genetic diversity among ILI cases at a secondary-care hospital in Islamabad during the 2025-2026 winter season.
analysis.methods: Among 170 qRT-PCR-tested cases, Influenza A was detected in 24.1%, SARS-CoV-2 in 1.17%, and Influenza B was not detected. Whole-genome sequencing of 21 Influenza A(H3N2) isolates revealed co-circulation of subclade K (52.4%), J.2.2 (28.6%), and J.2 (9.5%).
analysis.main_results: Influenza A positivity was slightly higher in females (25.0%), with highest burden in individuals aged 11-20 years. Phylogenetic analysis showed subclade K clustering with recent isolates from North America, Oceania, Europe, and WHO-recommended 2026-2027 Northern Hemisphere H3N2 vaccine strains, whereas J.2 and J.2.2 aligned with earlier vaccine-like strains. NA analysis showed predominance of clade B.4.2.2 associated with K-lineage and relatedness to recent North American strains. Subclade K exhibited conserved HA substitutions (K2N, S144N, N158D, I160K, Q173R, T328A) and HA2 S49N with limited variation. No antiviral resistance mutations were detected.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Overall, findings demonstrate predominance and genetic stability of H3N2 subclade K and support continuous genomic surveillance for vaccine strain selection and influenza preparedness.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The study highlights the importance of genomic surveillance in Pakistan for tracking influenza virus evolution and informing vaccine strategies, particularly given the predominance of subclade K, which aligns with recent global strains and recommended vaccine components.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study was conducted at a single secondary-care hospital in Islamabad, which may limit generalizability to other regions or populations. However, the use of whole-genome sequencing and phylogenetic analysis provides strong evidence for the genetic characterization of circulating strains.

analysis.summary_en: This study conducted molecular surveillance and genomic characterization of Influenza A(H3N2) viruses from a secondary-care site in Pakistan during the 2025-2026 winter season. Among 170 ILI cases, Influenza A was detected in 24.1%, with highest positivity in females and individuals aged 11-20 years. Whole-genome sequencing of 21 isolates revealed co-circulation of subclade K (52.4%), J.2.2 (28.6%), and J.2 (9.5%). Phylogenetic analysis showed subclade K clustering with recent global isolates and WHO-recommended vaccine strains, while J.2 and J.2.2 aligned with earlier strains. Subclade K exhibited conserved HA substitutions and no antiviral resistance mutations. The findings underscore the predominance and genetic stability of H3N2 subclade K and emphasize the need for continuous genomic surveillance to guide vaccine strategies and influenza preparedness in Pakistan.

analysis.methods: The study evaluated HI antibody reactivity across 25 A(H3N2) viruses and antibody binding to recombinant hemagglutinins (HA), comparing participants with different vaccination histories.
analysis.main_results: HI antibody responses were poor across strains for participants vaccinated five compared to zero of five prior years, independent of pre-vaccination titre, and HA and HA-stem binding antibody titre-rises were likewise attenuated in the repeatedly vaccinated group.

analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to healthcare workers and may not generalize to other populations, but the evidence strength is high due to the direct comparison of well-defined groups and comprehensive analysis across multiple virus strains.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the impact of repeated influenza vaccination on antibody responses against A(H3N2) antigens. Comparing healthcare workers with zero versus five consecutive years of vaccination, the researchers found that repeated vaccination led to blunted rather than enhanced antibody responses. HI antibody responses were poor across 25 A(H3N2) viruses for the repeatedly vaccinated group, independent of pre-vaccination titres, and HA and HA-stem binding antibody rises were similarly attenuated. The results challenge the hypothesis that repeated vaccination promotes antibodies targeting conserved epitopes, suggesting instead that repeated vaccination broadly weakens immune responses. This has significant implications for influenza vaccine strategies, potentially indicating that frequent vaccination may reduce effectiveness against A(H3N2) strains.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Seasonal influenza causes up to 650,000 deaths annually and remains a persistent pandemic threat due to zoonotic strains crossing the species barrier. Current antivirals, which target neuraminidase or the viral polymerase, have limited efficacy and rapidly select for resistant variants, highlighting the urgent need for new therapeutic strategies.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study focused on the heterotrimeric influenza polymerase (FluPol), comprising PA, PB1, and PB2 subunits, which is essential for viral replication and harbors virus-specific protein-protein interfaces that are potential drug targets. The researchers targeted the highly conserved PA-PB1 interface, where the N-terminal peptide of PB1 binds the PA C-terminal domain with high affinity.
analysis.methods: Using phage display, the researchers identified PB1-derived peptides with enhanced affinity for PA and characterized their binding via biophysical methods and X-ray crystallography. To address peptide delivery challenges, they expressed these inhibitors intracellularly from synthetic mRNA formulated in lipid nanoparticles.
analysis.main_results: Lead peptides efficiently disrupted the PB1-PA interaction and inhibited polymerase activity in cell-based assays. The intracellularly expressed peptide inhibitors achieved robust inhibition of viral replication in cultured cells.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Disrupting the PA-PB1 interaction abrogates polymerase function, halting viral replication. This work establishes intracellularly expressed peptide inhibitors as a viable antiviral strategy and provides a generalizable framework for targeting essential protein-protein interactions of influenza and other RNA viruses.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings demonstrate a novel approach to inhibit influenza A virus replication by disrupting the PA-PB1 interaction using affinity-enhanced peptides delivered via mRNA-LNPs. This strategy could lead to the development of new antiviral therapies with reduced potential for resistance.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study was conducted in cultured cells, and further research is needed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of this approach in animal models and humans. The evidence strength is moderate due to the preprint nature of the study and the lack of in vivo validation.

analysis.summary_en: This study addresses the urgent need for new influenza therapeutics by targeting the conserved PA-PB1 interaction in the viral polymerase. Using phage display, the researchers identified affinity-enhanced PB1-derived peptides that disrupt this interaction, inhibiting polymerase activity and viral replication in cultured cells. By delivering these peptides intracellularly via mRNA-LNPs, they achieved robust inhibition of influenza A virus replication. This work establishes a novel antiviral strategy with potential for broad applicability against influenza and other RNA viruses, though further validation in animal models and humans is needed.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Influenza A(H3N2) remains a significant public health threat due to its rapid antigenic drift, which often compromises vaccine effectiveness.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This study characterized the molecular and epidemiological profile of hemagglutinin (HA) variants circulating in Western Mexico throughout 2022.
analysis.methods: Sanger sequencing of the HA gene identified 64 amino acid substitutions, with 85.9% of the substitutions located in the HA1 subunit, primarily within the receptor-binding domain (RBD). Homology modeling and molecular docking were performed on five representative variants: C156S, D158N, Y159N, C136S, and L227P.
analysis.main_results: All variants exhibited a slight decrease in binding affinity for sialic acid compared to the 1HGE reference.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: These structural findings suggest that contemporary mutations in the RBD may contribute to changes in receptor-binding interactions while preserving key structural features associated with host cell attachment.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The molecular characterization of HA variants provides insights into the evolution of influenza A(H3N2) in Western Mexico, which can inform surveillance and vaccine strain selection.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's evidence strength is moderate, as it relies on a single year of data and limited structural modeling, but the findings are supported by direct sequencing and computational analyses.

analysis.summary_en: This study characterized the molecular and epidemiological profile of influenza A(H3N2) hemagglutinin variants in Western Mexico during 2022. Among 476 positive cases, A(H3N2) was predominant (88%), with peaks in early and late 2022. Sanger sequencing identified 64 amino acid substitutions, primarily in the HA1 subunit's receptor-binding domain. Structural modeling of five variants showed slight decreases in sialic acid binding affinity, with key residues like Glu190 and His183 maintaining critical interactions. The findings highlight the impact of contemporary mutations on receptor binding while preserving essential structural features, informing surveillance and vaccine strategies.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The rapid evolution of Influenza A(H3N2) requires constant global monitoring, and this study aimed to analyze the genomic characteristics and first introduction of the emerging subclade K (J.2.4.1) in Ecuador.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This study analyzed the hemagglutinin (HA) protein of an Influenza A(H3N2) strain isolated from an Ecuadorian patient, utilizing publicly available data to trace its intercontinental movement.
analysis.methods: A Bayesian phylogenetic reconstruction was performed using BEAST v1.10.4 with 251 global sequences, a molecular clock was applied to estimate the time of most recent common ancestor (TMRCA), and substitutions were screened using the FluSurver tool.
analysis.main_results: Phylogenetic analysis clustered the Ecuadorian isolate within a monophyletic group of European origin (Northern Spain), with the estimated introduction occurring in late November 2025, and molecular screening identified HA1 substitutions including S160N, N174D, I176K, Q189R, and Y211F, with S160N associated with the creation of a potential N-glycosylation site and the NA protein harboring the N358D substitution.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The introduction of subclade K into South America illustrates the high efficiency of transatlantic travel as a conduit for viral dispersal, and this study supports the use of open-access genomic surveillance as a critical sentinel tool for global health security.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings highlight the importance of genomic surveillance for early detection of emerging influenza strains and the role of international travel in viral spread, which can inform public health strategies for pandemic preparedness and response.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is based on a single isolate and limited to genomic analysis without clinical outcomes, but the use of global sequences and Bayesian methods provides moderate confidence in the findings.

analysis.summary_en: This study reports the first detection and genomic characterization of Influenza A(H3N2) subclade K (J.2.4.1) in Ecuador, tracing its introduction from Europe through phylogenetic analysis. The Ecuadorian isolate clustered with sequences from Northern Spain, with estimated introduction in late November 2025, coinciding with travel patterns. Key HA1 substitutions (S160N, N174D, I176K, Q189R, Y211F) and NA N358D were identified, with S160N creating a potential glycosylation site and N358D linked to neuraminidase inhibitor susceptibility. The findings demonstrate transatlantic travel's role in viral spread and underscore genomic surveillance's value for global health security.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The taxonomic status of the H17N10 and H18N11 influenza A viruses isolated from bats remains unclear due to the absence of quantitative classification criteria at this taxonomic level.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A total of 3328 representative IAV genomes, encompassing all eight protein-coding segments, were analysed.
analysis.methods: Various genetic distance-based metrics were assessed at the pairwise level, including intra- and intergroup nucleotide distances, dN/dS ratios, and transition/transversion ratios, to facilitate the differentiation of the Alphainfluenzavirus genus into distinct taxa.
analysis.main_results: Pairwise distances for seven of the eight segments (PB2, PB1, PA, NP, M, NA, NS) consistently differentiated the H17–H18 group from H1–H16, with intergroup nucleotide divergence consistently above ~25% and intragroup divergence substantially lower.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The consistent genomic patterns provide support for the hypothesis that H17N10 and H18N11 viruses may represent a separate species within the genus Alphainfluenzavirus, consistent with the hypothesis of ancient reassortment for the HA segment.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings contribute to the taxonomic classification of influenza viruses and may inform surveillance and evolutionary studies of bat influenza viruses.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence strength is high due to the large dataset and consistent genetic distance patterns, though the study is limited by the absence of reassortment compatibility data for all segments.

analysis.summary_en: This study assessed the taxonomic status of H17N10 and H18N11 influenza A viruses from bats by analyzing 3328 representative IAV genomes. Using genetic distance metrics, the researchers found consistent differentiation between the H17–H18 group and H1–H16 viruses across seven segments, with intergroup divergence above 25% and intragroup divergence lower. The HA segment showed a different pattern, suggesting ancient reassortment. The results support classifying H17N10 and H18N11 as a separate species within Alphainfluenzavirus, providing a quantitative basis for their taxonomic classification.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate how vaccination history, including frequency and recency, influences humoral responses to seasonal influenza vaccination, as these effects on standard serological endpoints were incompletely defined.
analysis.study_design_and_population: We analyzed paired pre- and post-vaccination hemagglutination inhibition and neuraminidase inhibition titers from 775 adults in the New Zealand SHIVERS-II cohort during the 2018 influenza season, relating these to vaccination histories from 2013–2017.
analysis.methods: Paired pre- and post-vaccination hemagglutination inhibition and neuraminidase inhibition titers were analyzed and related to vaccination histories (2013–2017) to assess immunogenicity metrics.
analysis.main_results: Post-vaccination titers increased across groups, but participants vaccinated more frequently were less likely to meet conventional ≥4-fold rise and seroconversion criteria, particularly for A/H3N2, despite higher absolute post-vaccination titers; longer intervals since the most recent vaccination were associated with higher probabilities of meeting these thresholds.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that vaccination frequency and recency shape measured humoral responses, highlighting that fold-rise-based immunogenicity metrics should be interpreted in the context of baseline immunity and immune history, which was a novel insight for understanding serological responses.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings inform that immunogenicity metrics should be interpreted considering vaccination history, which is crucial for evaluating vaccine efficacy and guiding vaccination strategies, though clinical protection was not assessed.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study did not assess clinical protection, limiting direct public health implications; however, the large sample size and robust serological methods provide moderate evidence strength for the observed immunological patterns.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated how vaccination history influences humoral responses to seasonal influenza vaccination in 775 New Zealand adults. Analyzing paired pre- and post-vaccination titers from 2018, researchers found that more frequent vaccination was associated with lower probabilities of meeting conventional seroconversion criteria, despite higher absolute post-vaccination titers, particularly for A/H3N2. Longer intervals since recent vaccination correlated with better serological responses. The findings highlight that fold-rise metrics must be interpreted in the context of baseline immunity and vaccination history, though clinical protection was not assessed. This provides important insights for evaluating vaccine immunogenicity and informing vaccination strategies.

The evidence strength is moderate, relying on model-based estimates and historical data.

analysis.scope_and_question: This systematic review and meta-analysis focused on seasonal influenza viruses (A(H1N1)pdm09, A(H3N2), B/Victoria, and historical B/Yamagata) in human populations. The central question was to quantify changes in influenza burden between pre-pandemic and intra-pandemic periods, specifically examining the impact of COVID-19-related non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) on influenza incidence.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The study followed PRISMA guidelines and was conducted within the RESPINOW project. It included 115 studies from 98 countries reporting absolute influenza case counts before and during the pandemic. Data extraction and quality assessment used a modified NHLBI tool for before-after studies. Influenza cases were normalized by reporting period length, and relative changes were estimated using incidence rate ratios. Subgroup analyses explored age, setting, hemisphere, human development index, influenza transmission zones, WHO regions, and viral strains.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The COVID-19 pandemic was associated with an unprecedented global reduction in influenza incidence, with a decline of −92% (95% CI: −94 to −90). Reductions were observed across all transmission zones and WHO regions, with larger decreases in high-income countries (−96%, 95% CI: −98 to −94) compared to low-income settings (−82%, 95% CI: −88 to −73). Age-specific declines were smaller among young children (<6 years: −66%, 95% CI: −79 to −45) than in adults aged 18–64 years (−80%, 95% CI: −90 to −63). Influenza A appeared to decline more strongly than influenza B.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The study noted significant geographic variation in influenza reductions, ranging from near-elimination in some countries to more modest declines (e.g., South Korea: −61%, 95% CI: −79 to −26). Data limitations and the need for robust epidemiological indicators were highlighted, particularly regarding the variability in NPI implementation and compliance across settings. The study did not address potential mechanisms behind differential impacts by age or viral type.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The findings underscore the importance of strengthened, integrated global surveillance to inform future pandemic responses. There is a need for robust epidemiological indicators to better understand the impact of NPIs on respiratory viruses and to develop targeted interventions. Future research should explore the factors contributing to geographic and demographic variations in influenza burden during the pandemic.

analysis.summary_en: This systematic review and meta-analysis quantified the impact of COVID-19-related non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) on seasonal influenza burden. Analyzing 115 studies from 98 countries, the study found a global reduction in influenza incidence of −92% (95% CI: −94 to −90) during the pandemic. Reductions varied geographically, with larger decreases in high-income countries (−96%) compared to low-income settings (−82%). Age-specific declines were smaller in young children (<6 years: −66%) than in adults (18–64 years: −80%), and influenza A declined more strongly than influenza B. The study highlights the need for strengthened global surveillance to inform future pandemic responses and understand the differential impacts of NPIs.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Evidence suggests that a substantial part of influenza-related morbidity and mortality is due to cardiovascular events, and limited population-level evidence exists regarding whether seasonal influenza vaccination is associated with a lower risk of ischemic stroke in older adults with diabetes.
analysis.study_design_and_population: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using data from the Regional Health Information Platform, including 131,045 diabetic adults aged ≥ 60 y alive and free of prior IS as of January 1, 2022, followed until IS occurrence, death, or July 31, 2022.
analysis.methods: The primary outcome was first-ever IS; vaccination exposure was receipt of the 2021/22 seasonal inactivated influenza vaccine; subdistribution hazard ratios (sHR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) were estimated using Fine-Gray competing risk models, with death as a competing risk.
analysis.main_results: During 75,593 person-years of follow-up over approximately 7 months, 1,427 IS cases occurred (incidence rate: 18.9 per 1,000 person-years); after multivariable adjustment, influenza vaccination was associated with a 15% reduced IS risk within 7 months of follow-up (adjusted sHR = 0.85; 95% CI: 0.76-0.95).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The inverse association was consistent across influenza activity phases and was most pronounced during high antigenic similarity epidemic periods and among patients with coronary heart disease; the negative control analysis showed no association between pneumococcal vaccination and IS risk.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Seasonal influenza vaccination was associated with a significantly reduced risk of incident IS within 7 months among older adults with diabetes, supporting its potential inclusion as a low-cost stroke prevention strategy in this high-risk population.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: Randomized controlled trials are warranted to confirm causality; the evidence strength is moderate due to the observational design and potential residual confounding.

analysis.summary_en: This retrospective cohort study investigated the association between seasonal influenza vaccination and ischemic stroke (IS) risk in older adults with diabetes. Among 131,045 participants, 54,617 received influenza vaccination. Over 75,593 person-years of follow-up, 1,427 IS cases occurred. Vaccination was associated with a 15% reduced IS risk (adjusted sHR = 0.85; 95% CI: 0.76-0.95), with stronger effects during high antigenic similarity periods and in patients with coronary heart disease. No association was found with pneumococcal vaccination. The findings suggest influenza vaccination may be a low-cost stroke prevention strategy in this high-risk population, though randomized trials are needed to confirm causality.

analysis.scope_and_question: This review examines the role of CD4+ T cell repertoire and immune memory mechanisms in vaccination and infection immunity against respiratory viruses, specifically focusing on SARS-CoV-2 and influenza virus immunity.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: This review summarizes current evidence on how CD4+ T cell subsets shape the magnitude, breadth, and durability of immunity to SARS-CoV-2 and influenza virus.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: mRNA vaccines elicit a potent Th1/Tfh1-biased response that generates high-affinity neutralizing antibodies and cytotoxic CD4+ T cells (CD4-CTLs) with stem-cell memory properties. Natural infection additionally establishes tissue-resident memory CD4+ T cells (CD4 TRMs) at respiratory mucosal surfaces. T cell immunity proves more resilient than neutralizing antibodies against Variants of Concern, as many memory T cell epitopes are conserved across variants.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The strong type I bias in mRNA vaccines may come at the cost of long-term maintenance of humoral memory. Current intramuscular vaccines fail to efficiently recapitulate tissue-resident memory CD4+ T cells at respiratory mucosal surfaces established by natural infection.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: These observations argue for a fundamental shift in vaccine design toward mucosal delivery and conserved-epitope antigens to achieve durable, broadly cross-reactive protection.

analysis.summary_en: This review examines CD4+ T cell mechanisms in respiratory virus immunity, comparing vaccine and infection responses. It finds mRNA vaccines induce potent Th1/Tfh1-biased responses with high-affinity antibodies and CD4-CTLs, but may compromise long-term humoral memory. Natural infection establishes superior mucosal tissue-resident memory CD4+ T cells. T cell immunity shows greater resilience against variants than antibodies due to conserved epitopes and cross-reactive T cells from prior exposures. The review advocates for mucosal vaccine delivery and conserved-epitope antigens to improve durable protection.

analysis.scope_and_question: The review focuses on seasonal influenza viruses as a significant national health security threat, particularly for vulnerable populations, and explores pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) as a complementary strategy to reduce transmission and disease severity when existing control measures are insufficient.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The manuscript outlines the Biomedical Advanced Research and Development Authority's (BARDA's) target product profile (TPP) for a long-acting influenza PrEP product, reviews the current development landscape, and models the potential impact of early PrEP deployment using agent-based modeling in a synthetic population of 19.5 million people across pandemic scenarios resembling the 1918, 1968, and 2009 influenza pandemics.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Clinical studies support PrEP therapeutics as a promising complementary strategy to reduce influenza transmission and disease severity. Simulations showed that early deployment of a 70%–effective PrEP reduced cumulative and peak infections, delayed the epidemic peak, and provided the greatest benefit in less transmissible pandemics; at 40–50% coverage, PrEP fully mitigated a 2009-like pandemic and substantially reduced transmission in 1918- and 1968-like scenarios.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The gap in protection is especially pronounced early in a pandemic when a well-matched vaccine may not yet be available, as well as in populations unable to mount an optimal vaccine response. The TPP defines key characteristics of an effective PrEP option, but the review does not address potential controversies or specific evidence gaps beyond these limitations.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Integrating PrEP into influenza prevention strategies could improve control of virus spread, strengthen protection for high-risk groups, and significantly reduce the overall public health impact of seasonal and pandemic influenza. The TPP emphasizes a strong safety profile, direct-acting antiviral mechanism, at least 70% reduction in symptomatic infection risk, and single-dose, season-long protection to optimize adherence.

analysis.summary_en: This review examines pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) as a complementary strategy for seasonal influenza prevention, addressing gaps in protection for vulnerable populations, especially during early pandemics or in suboptimal vaccine responders. The Biomedical Advanced Research and Development Authority's (BARDA) target product profile (TPP) outlines key characteristics for an effective PrEP, including 70% efficacy, single-dose season-long protection, and strong safety. Agent-based modeling in 19.5 million people across 1918, 1968, and 2009 pandemic scenarios demonstrated that early PrEP deployment reduced infections, delayed epidemic peaks, and fully mitigated a 2009-like pandemic at 40-50% coverage. The review concludes that integrating PrEP could significantly reduce influenza transmission and public health impact, though challenges remain in vaccine-mismatched scenarios and for high-risk groups.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Seasonal influenza vaccination has been shown to reduce the risk of influenza and severe complications among children aged 6 months and older.
analysis.study_design_and_population: We estimated influenza vaccine effectiveness (VE) against pediatric death from 2016 to 2017 through 2024 to 2025.
analysis.methods: We conducted a case-cohort analysis comparing current season influenza vaccination status among reported influenza-associated pediatric deaths with survey estimates of influenza vaccination coverage in pediatric age groups. We estimated vaccination odds ratios (OR) and 95% CIs from logistic regression comparing influenza vaccination among children who died with vaccination coverage in comparison cohorts. VE was calculated as (1 - OR) × 100.
analysis.main_results: From August 2016 through July 2025, 1234 laboratory-confirmed influenza-associated pediatric deaths were reported among children aged 6 months to 17 years. Of 1086 reported deaths with influenza vaccination information, 124 (23%) of 530 children with underlying medical conditions and 70 (13%) of 556 children without known conditions were fully vaccinated against influenza. Average influenza vaccination coverage in survey cohorts was 49%. VE was 80% (95% CI 75-84) overall, 77% (95% CI 71-82) among children with underlying medical conditions and 87% (95% CI 84-89) among children without known conditions.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Influenza vaccination reduced risk of fatal influenza among children with or without known underlying medical conditions.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings support the importance of influenza vaccination in reducing pediatric mortality, particularly for children with underlying medical conditions.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study relied on surveillance case reports and survey estimates, which may introduce reporting bias. The evidence strength is moderate due to the observational design and potential confounding factors.

analysis.summary_en: This study estimated influenza vaccine effectiveness (VE) against pediatric death in the United States from 2016 to 2025. Using a case-cohort analysis, researchers compared vaccination status among 1234 laboratory-confirmed influenza-associated pediatric deaths with survey coverage estimates. Overall VE was 80%, with 77% effectiveness in children with underlying medical conditions and 87% in those without. The findings demonstrate that influenza vaccination significantly reduces the risk of fatal influenza in children, supporting its importance in pediatric public health strategies.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Timely monitoring of maternal vaccination is essential for guiding immunization strategies, but ongoing pregnancies are usually not identified in health registries, resulting in delayed surveillance.
analysis.study_design_and_population: We evaluated a registry-based method using routinely collected pregnancy-specific ultrasound procedure codes introduced in 2022 to identify ongoing pregnancies and demonstrate feasibility of timely vaccination surveillance, using influenza vaccination as an example.
analysis.methods: We linked population-based registry data from the Medical Birth Registry of Norway, the Norwegian Patient Register, and the Immunisation Registry. Ongoing pregnancies in the Norwegian Patient Register were identified using either second-trimester ultrasound procedure codes (Scenario 1) or a combination of first- and second-trimester codes with adjustments for pregnancy loss and non-attendance (Scenario 2).
analysis.main_results: A total of 26,996 and 27,940 pregnant women were identified using Scenarios 1 and 2, respectively, compared with 27,513 using Medical Birth Registry data. Monthly vaccination uptake estimates deviated by less than 1.5% from the gold standard. Cumulative vaccination uptake was 27.1% (7328/26,996) and 26.9% (7503/27,940) for Scenarios 1 and 2, compared with 27.8% (7656/27,513) using Medical Birth Registry data.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Ongoing pregnancies can be identified through ultrasound procedure codes from administrative healthcare data, enabling robust and timely vaccination surveillance during pregnancy. The approach supports near real-time vaccination monitoring and might be applicable to broader antenatal care surveillance in general.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: This method enables near real-time monitoring of maternal vaccination uptake, which can inform timely public health interventions and policy adjustments during influenza seasons.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study relies on administrative healthcare data and specific ultrasound procedure codes, which may not capture all pregnancies or account for all biases in reporting. The evidence strength is moderate due to potential underreporting and the limited scope of the influenza season examined.

analysis.summary_en: This Norwegian registry study assessed a method to identify ongoing pregnancies using routine ultrasound procedure codes for timely maternal vaccination surveillance. By linking registry data from the Medical Birth Registry of Norway, the Norwegian Patient Register, and the Immunisation Registry, the authors evaluated two scenarios for identifying pregnancies: second-trimester ultrasound codes alone or combined first- and second-trimester codes with adjustments. The method identified 26,996 to 27,940 pregnant women, closely matching the 27,513 identified by the gold-standard Medical Birth Registry data. Monthly influenza vaccination uptake estimates deviated by less than 1.5% from the gold standard, and cumulative uptake ranged from 26.9% to 27.1% across scenarios, compared to 27.8% using the gold standard. The authors conclude that ultrasound procedure codes can enable robust and timely vaccination surveillance during pregnancy, supporting near real-time monitoring applicable to broader antenatal care surveillance.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Persons with occupational exposure to swine might be at disproportionate risk for zoonotic swine influenza A virus.
analysis.study_design_and_population: To evaluate human antibody responses, we tested serum or plasma from swine veterinarian, farm employee, and general population cohorts by hemagglutination inhibition assays against representative swine and human seasonal influenza vaccine strains.
analysis.methods: We analyzed hemagglutination inhibition data by antigenic cartography to assess strain relationships and reproduction number modeling to evaluate pandemic potential using age-stratified immunity profiles.
analysis.main_results: Occupationally exposed groups had lower human seasonal vaccine uptake (45.5% vs. 70%) and lower odds of seropositivity to several H1 and H3 strains from swine than did general population cohorts. analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Multiple strains required lower reproduction number thresholds for pandemic spread (1.09-1.35) than recorded pandemic strains (1.46-1.80), demonstrating that population immunity gaps heighten zoonotic risk to circulating swine H1 and H3 strains.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings indicate that occupational exposure to swine may increase zoonotic risk, and the antigenic drift and lower reproduction number thresholds highlight the need for enhanced surveillance and vaccination strategies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study relied on hemagglutination inhibition assays and modeling, which may not capture all aspects of immune response or pandemic potential. The evidence strength is moderate due to the observational design and reliance on serological data.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated antibody profiles to swine influenza A viruses in occupationally exposed and general populations. Swine veterinarians and farm employees showed lower vaccine uptake and seropositivity to swine H1 and H3 strains compared to the general population. One swine strain exhibited significant antigenic drift, and multiple strains had lower reproduction number thresholds for pandemic spread, indicating heightened zoonotic risk due to population immunity gaps. The findings underscore the need for targeted surveillance and vaccination strategies to mitigate zoonotic transmission.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addressed the public-health need to characterize the first documented human infection with a swine-origin influenza A(H1N2)v virus in mainland China and to inform prevention and control guidance for such emerging zoonoses.

analysis.summary_en: This case report describes the first documented human infection with a swine-origin influenza A(H1N2)v virus in mainland China, identified through influenza-like illness surveillance in Kunming, Yunnan, in 2025. The investigation confirmed N2-subtype positivity in lung tissue from a deceased pig and found no evidence of human-to-human transmission or secondary cases among 30 close contacts. The authors concluded that deceased pigs were the likely source and recommended enhanced surveillance of novel influenza subtypes and improved swine influenza vaccination to prevent future human infections.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Influenza viruses cause seasonal epidemics, and current vaccines do not fully protect against them. This study focuses on long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), which are RNA molecules that do not code for proteins but play crucial roles in various biological processes.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study identified 17 lncRNAs altered by the influenza virus, with a focus on SNHG15's role in enhancing influenza virus infection.
analysis.methods: Knockdown of SNHG15 using CRISPR interference and RNA interference reduced influenza virus infection, while overexpression of SNHG15 increased virus replication. RNA pull-down and mass spectrometry identified Rab-like protein 2A (RABL2A) as an interacting partner of SNHG15.
analysis.main_results: Among the altered lncRNAs, SNHG15 was found to enhance influenza virus infection. Knockdown of SNHG15 reduced influenza virus infection, while overexpression increased virus replication. Both SNHG15 and RABL2A facilitated influenza virus internalization.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that SNHG15 enhances influenza A virus infection through its interactions with miR-153 and RABL2A. The novelty lies in identifying this specific molecular mechanism involving lncRNAs in influenza virus infection.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings could inform the development of novel therapeutic strategies targeting SNHG15 or its interacting partners to inhibit influenza virus infection and improve vaccine efficacy.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is based on in vitro experiments and may not fully represent in vivo conditions. The evidence strength is moderate due to the limited scope of the study and the need for further validation in animal models and clinical settings.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the role of long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) in influenza virus infection, identifying SNHG15 as a key enhancer. The researchers found that SNHG15 promotes influenza virus infection by interacting with miR-153 and RABL2A. Knockdown of SNHG15 reduced infection, while overexpression increased replication. These findings suggest potential therapeutic targets for improving influenza treatment and vaccine development.

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to assess vaccine literacy, knowledge, and acceptance among Palestinian university students and identify associated factors with vaccine acceptance, addressing the scarcity of data on vaccine literacy and acceptance among university students in Palestine.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A cross-sectional study was conducted at multiple universities across the West Bank, Palestine, during the 2025–2026 academic year, involving 633 university students who completed a structured, self-administered questionnaire distributed via Google Forms.
analysis.methods: Non-parametric group comparisons were performed using the Mann–Whitney U test and Chi-square test, while Spearman correlation and multivariable linear regression were used to identify predictors of vaccine acceptance.
analysis.main_results: The median age of participants was 19 years (IQR: 18–21), and 72.4% were female; median scores were moderate across all domains: vaccine knowledge 5.0/10 (IQR: 3.0–6.0), vaccine literacy 3.50/5 (IQR: 3.0–3.88), and vaccine acceptance 3.11/5 (IQR: 2.78–3.56); while 67.8% of students reported receiving recommended vaccines in the past five years, seasonal influenza vaccination was critically low at 9.5%.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Health-related students scored significantly higher than non-health students in knowledge, literacy, acceptance, vaccine uptake, and trust in official sources (all p ≤ 0.010), and female students demonstrated higher knowledge (p = 0.021) and literacy scores (p < 0.05).
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings highlight the need for targeted interventions to improve vaccine literacy and acceptance among university students in Palestine, particularly for seasonal influenza vaccination, which remains critically low.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study was limited by its cross-sectional design, which cannot establish causality, and the reliance on self-reported data, which may introduce recall bias; however, the large sample size and validated instruments provide moderate evidence strength.

analysis.summary_en: This cross-sectional study assessed vaccine literacy, knowledge, and acceptance among 633 Palestinian university students during the 2025–2026 academic year. The median age was 19 years, with 72.4% female participants. Median scores were moderate: vaccine knowledge 5.0/10, literacy 3.50/5, and acceptance 3.11/5. While 67.8% reported receiving recommended vaccines, seasonal influenza vaccination was critically low at 9.5%. Health-related students scored significantly higher than non-health students in all domains (p ≤ 0.010), and female students showed higher knowledge and literacy (p < 0.05). The findings underscore the need for targeted interventions to improve vaccine literacy and acceptance, particularly for seasonal influenza.

analysis.summary_en: This study examines how fear and social influence jointly and individually affect COVID-19 vaccine acceptance, focusing on the Oxford–AstraZeneca vaccine. Social influence emerged as the strongest predictor across all models, substantially reducing the explanatory power of fear when considered jointly. The findings suggest that health communication strategies should prioritize credible institutional messaging and trusted influencers over fear-based appeals. The study has limitations, including its focus on Spain and a specific vaccine type during a particular time period, and recommends replication in other contexts.
