analysis.research_question_and_background: Seasonal influenza vaccine strain selection remains challenging because circulating viruses may drift after vaccine recommendations are made.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This study presents FluEvoFormer, a structure-guided generative foundation model for prospective influenza antigenic evolution forecasting and vaccine strain ranking. A rolling retrospective evaluation was performed for target seasons involving the influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 virus and influenza A(H3N2) virus.
analysis.methods: The framework jointly encodes hemagglutinin and neuraminidase sequences and incorporates residue-contact graphs. Separate prediction heads estimate future viral dominance and the vaccine–virus antigenic match. Controlled future-like variant stress testing, uncertainty adjustments, and clade balancing are then used to rank vaccine candidates.
analysis.main_results: FluEvoFormer achieved the lowest held-out antigenicity prediction error, with mean absolute error (MAE) values of 0.389 for the combined historical influenza A(H1N1) virus corpus and 0.456 for the influenza A(H3N2) virus corpus. It also improved the future dominance prediction, with Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence values of 0.255 and 0.289, respectively. The model selected candidates with higher empirical normalized coverage scores in seven out of 10 influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 virus seasons and nine out of 10 influenza A(H3N2) virus seasons.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The predicted coverage score showed a strong positive correlation with external vaccine-effectiveness estimates. These findings support FluEvoFormer as a computational decision-support framework for prioritizing influenza vaccine candidates before downstream laboratory and public health evaluations.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: FluEvoFormer provides a computational tool to improve influenza vaccine strain selection by forecasting antigenic evolution and ranking candidates, potentially enhancing vaccine effectiveness and public health responses.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is based on retrospective evaluation and historical data, which may not fully capture future viral evolution dynamics. The evidence strength is moderate due to the abstract-only nature and reliance on computational modeling without real-world validation.

analysis.summary_en: FluEvoFormer is a structure-guided generative foundation model designed to forecast influenza antigenic evolution and rank vaccine candidates. It jointly encodes hemagglutinin and neuraminidase sequences with residue-contact graphs, using separate prediction heads for viral dominance and antigenic match. Evaluated retrospectively for influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 and A(H3N2) viruses, FluEvoFormer achieved low antigenicity prediction errors (MAE: 0.389 and 0.456) and improved dominance prediction (KL divergence: 0.255 and 0.289). It selected higher coverage candidates in most seasons, with strong correlation to vaccine effectiveness. This computational framework supports early prioritization of vaccine strains before laboratory and public health evaluations.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Accurate short-term forecasts of influenza activity are critical for public health preparedness but remain challenging with classical statistical models that depend on long historical data and often fail under data scarcity.
analysis.study_design_and_population: We analyzed 605 weeks of influenza surveillance data from Hong Kong (2014–2025), including consultation rates, laboratory detections, hospital admissions, severe cases, and school outbreaks.
analysis.methods: Six TSFMs (Google TimesFM, Amazon Chronos, IBM Granite Tiny Time Mixers [TTM], Timer-XL, Moirai-MoE, and UniTS) were compared with OLS, GLM, SARIMA, and empirical Bayesian models in a rolling-origin design generating one- to four-week forecasts. Forecast accuracy was evaluated using R2, RMSE, symmetric MAPE, weighted interval score (WIS) and multivariable residual diagnostics.
analysis.main_results: Chronos, TimesFM, and SARIMA achieved the best overall one-week performance (R2 0.88–0.89; RMSE 30.6–31.3), significantly outperforming OLS (R2 0.78; p < 0.0001) and GLM (R2 0.79; p < 0.0001). Chronos outperformed other models in two-to-four-week performance. Chronos produced credible forecasts of the multivariate influenza surveillance predictions up to three weeks (R2 ≥ 0.50; p < 0.05), whereas classical models fell below threshold beyond two weeks. TSFMs required as low as eight weeks of input data to achieve R2 ≥ 0.50, compared to at least 297 weeks for classical models.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: TSFMs deliver comparatively more accurate, well-calibrated, and data-efficient epidemic forecasts, capturing temporal and inter-variable dependencies than classical regression models. Their ability to generate more reliable forecasts from minimal historical data compared to classical approaches supports their potential for rapid deployment in seasonal influenza surveillance and emerging pandemics such as COVID-19.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that TSFMs can enhance public health preparedness by providing reliable influenza forecasts with minimal data, enabling timely resource allocation and intervention strategies during seasonal outbreaks and pandemics.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study was conducted using surveillance data from a single geographic region (Hong Kong), which may limit generalizability to other populations with different influenza dynamics. The evidence strength is high due to the large dataset size, rigorous comparative design, and statistically significant results.

analysis.summary_en: This study compared time-series foundation models (TSFMs) with classical statistical models for influenza forecasting using 11 years of surveillance data from Hong Kong. Six TSFMs (including Chronos, TimesFM, and TTM) were evaluated against OLS, GLM, SARIMA, and Bayesian models for one- to four-week forecasts. Chronos achieved the best overall performance, with R2 values of 0.88–0.89 for one-week forecasts and credible predictions up to three weeks (R2 ≥ 0.50). TSFMs required only eight weeks of data to achieve acceptable accuracy, compared to 297 weeks for classical models. The findings demonstrate that TSFMs offer superior accuracy, data efficiency, and reliability for influenza forecasting, with potential applications in seasonal surveillance and pandemic response.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Influenza contributes to significant disease burden worldwide, and young infants are at an increased risk of severe influenza infection. Maternal antibodies transferred across the placenta and through breast milk confer anti-influenza immunity to the newborn.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved a longitudinal birth cohort to analyze influenza-specific antibodies across 21 different antigens in breast milk and serum compartments.
analysis.methods: Comprehensive systems serological analysis was performed to assess antibody-dependent complement deposition (ADCD), FcγR binding, FcαR binding, and IgM levels in breast milk and serum samples.
analysis.main_results: Maternal influenza vaccination was associated with enhanced ADCD and FcγR binding in breast milk at two weeks postpartum, with effects stratified by trimester of vaccination. Longitudinal analysis revealed postpartum shifts toward increased FcγR binding and decreased ADCD activity and IgM levels.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that maternal influenza vaccination confers infant protection via breast milk to augment placental antibody transfer, and the functional capacity of these protective antibodies could be enhanced with prolonged breastfeeding.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings suggest that maternal vaccination and breastfeeding strategies could be optimized to enhance infant protection against influenza, with baseline ADCD activity in breast milk and serum IgG1 levels identified as signatures of resistance to infection.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to observational data from a single birth cohort, but the comprehensive systems serological approach and longitudinal design provide moderate evidence for the protective role of breast milk antibodies.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated how maternal influenza vaccination shapes breast milk antibody profiles and their contribution to infant protection. Using a longitudinal birth cohort, the researchers found that maternal vaccination enhanced functional antibody activities in breast milk, with effects varying by trimester of vaccination. Longitudinal analysis revealed postpartum shifts in antibody functions, and baseline ADCD activity and serum IgG1 levels were identified as protective signatures. The multivariate model combining milk and serum compartments showed greater predictive power, suggesting both antibody transfer routes bolster infant immunity. These findings support the importance of maternal vaccination and prolonged breastfeeding for infant influenza protection.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addresses an incomplete understanding of influenza transmission dynamics, particularly the role of asymptomatic infections that often evade detection and the factors shaping household spread.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The research used a household cohort study conducted over three consecutive influenza seasons in rural and urban South Africa, involving repeated pre-season serum collection and twice-weekly virological testing regardless of symptoms.
analysis.methods: A subtype/lineage-specific influenza household transmission model was developed to incorporate time-resolved viral shedding data across the full clinical spectrum of infections, enabling separation of household and community exposure effects, pre-season immunity, and age influences on transmission.
analysis.main_results: Viral shedding intensity, measured by cycle threshold values from infected household members, was significantly associated with increased transmission risk for all four influenza subtypes/lineages studied.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Pre-season hemagglutination inhibition titers above 1:40 were linked to lower infection risk for A(H1N1)pdm09, A(H3N2), and B/Victoria but not B/Yamagata, while children showed higher susceptibility and longer shedding durations than adults across all subtypes, even after adjusting for pre-season immunity.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings highlight the importance of viral shedding intensity and age-specific susceptibility in influenza transmission, suggesting that immune mechanisms beyond hemagglutination inhibition titers may play key roles in modulating susceptibility and spread.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on abstract-only evidence and the absence of detailed methodological or statistical reporting, which constrains the strength of the conclusions drawn.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates influenza transmission dynamics within households in South Africa over three consecutive seasons, leveraging pre-season immunity data and twice-weekly virological testing to capture asymptomatic and symptomatic infections. Using a subtype-specific transmission model, the authors demonstrate that viral shedding intensity strongly correlates with transmission risk across all four influenza subtypes/lineages. Pre-season hemagglutination inhibition titers above 1:40 were associated with reduced infection risk for A(H1N1)pdm09, A(H3N2), and B/Victoria but not B/Yamagata, while children exhibited higher susceptibility and prolonged shedding durations than adults, independent of pre-season immunity. These results underscore the need to explore immune mechanisms beyond hemagglutination inhibition titers and suggest that age-specific factors critically shape household transmission dynamics.

analysis.scope_and_question: The review focuses on RNA virus reverse genetics technology, covering its development, applications, and future prospects. The central question involves understanding how this technology enables the rescue of infectious virions from cloned cDNA and its role in mapping viral genotype-phenotype relationships, dissecting RNA viral life cycles, and developing antiviral countermeasures.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: This is a systematic review that summarizes the evolution, technical framework, and optimization strategies of RNA virus reverse genetics. It uses three prototype viruses representing all major RNA genome types: SARS-CoV-2 (+ssRNA), Newcastle disease virus (NDV), and influenza A virus. The review elaborates on core modules such as infectious clone construction, promoter systems, ribozymes, and solutions for large unstable genomes.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The consensus is that RNA virus reverse genetics is an irreplaceable tool for vaccine development, pathogenesis research, virus-host interaction analysis, and high-throughput antiviral screening. The review highlights its applications across different RNA virus types and emphasizes its importance in basic virology, vaccine innovation, and antiviral design.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: Current bottlenecks include low rescue efficiency, cDNA genetic instability, and biosafety hazards. The review identifies these as key challenges that need to be addressed to advance the field. Additionally, there is a need for more standardized modular tools and biosafety engineering to overcome these limitations.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Future advances should integrate CRISPR/Cas editing, standardized modular tools, biosafety engineering, AI, and big data to improve the efficiency and safety of RNA virus reverse genetics. The review also suggests establishing a three-tier antiviral screening pipeline and developing non-infectious surrogate platforms to address current limitations.

analysis.summary_en: This review systematically examines RNA virus reverse genetics technology, highlighting its evolution, technical frameworks, and optimization strategies across major RNA genome types. It emphasizes the technology's critical role in vaccine development, pathogenesis research, and antiviral screening. Despite its applications, current bottlenecks such as low rescue efficiency and biosafety hazards are identified. Future directions include integrating CRISPR/Cas editing, AI, and standardized tools to enhance efficiency and safety. The review provides comprehensive insights for advancing basic virology and antiviral design.

analysis.study_design_and_population: IMPRINT is a prospective birth cohort of healthy mothers and children in Cincinnati, Ohio. Mothers are enrolled in the third trimester and followed with their child for at least three years with an enrollment goal of 1,500 mother-child pairs.

Serum is collected from mothers at enrollment and each summer post-enrollment. analysis.summary_en: The Influenza IMPRINT Cohort study aims to understand how early exposures to influenza antigens shape immune responses later in life. The study uses advanced methodologies to track influenza infections and vaccinations, providing a novel framework to analyze immunologic imprinting. Despite challenges in enrollment, the cohort demonstrates successful follow-up, offering insights into the impact of early influenza exposures on long-term immunity. The findings may inform the development of more effective influenza vaccines by addressing gaps in influenza epidemiology and immunology.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Immunogenicity to influenza vaccination is often impaired in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), and the role of the gut microbiota and its metabolic output in modulating this response remains underexplored.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A cross-sectional observational pilot study was conducted at Ramathibodi Hospital between May 2021 and July 2022, enrolling 62 participants with SLE who had received either a boosted dose or a standard dose of a quadrivalent influenza vaccine.
analysis.methods: We analyzed fecal 16 S rDNA and metabolomic profiles using liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry to identify signatures associated with seroconversion (determined using the hemagglutination inhibition assay).
analysis.main_results: The overall gut microbiota patterns were similar in both groups; however, the genus Bacteroides was significantly associated with seroconversion to A(H1N1) and A(H3N2) (P < 0.05). Metabolomic analysis identified upregulation of 1,5-anhydro-D-glucitol and L-cysteic acid in seroconverters, whereas neopterin was significantly elevated in nonresponders.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: These results suggest that the gut–immune axis may play a modulatory role in vaccine responses and may provide potential non-invasive biomarkers that can identify patients at risk of suboptimal influenza protection.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings identify specific gut microbial taxa and fecal metabolites, particularly 1,5-anhydro-D-glucitol, which are significantly associated with influenza vaccine immunogenicity in SLE patients, potentially informing personalized vaccination strategies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is a pilot with a small sample size (n=62), and the cross-sectional design limits causal inference; however, the targeted analysis of gut microbiota and metabolites provides moderate evidence for their association with vaccine response.

analysis.summary_en: This cross-sectional observational pilot study investigated gut microbiota and metabolome patterns as potential biomarkers for influenza vaccine immunogenicity in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Conducted at Ramathibodi Hospital with 62 SLE patients, the study analyzed fecal samples using 16 S rDNA sequencing and metabolomics. Key findings included significant associations between the Bacteroides genus and seroconversion to A(H1N1) and A(H3N2), as well as elevated levels of 1,5-anhydro-D-glucitol and L-cysteic acid in seroconverters. The study suggests the gut-immune axis may modulate vaccine responses, offering potential non-invasive biomarkers for identifying patients at risk of suboptimal protection. While limited by its small sample size and cross-sectional design, the findings provide moderate evidence for the role of gut microbiota in influenza vaccine immunogenicity.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Because viruses depend on host cells for replication and spread, extensive research has identified host factors that facilitate infection, but these studies do not fully capture the complexity of infection in vivo.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A team of researchers generated a library of CRISPR-Cas9-engineered knockout mice and used it to identify host genes that influence susceptibility to influenza A virus infection in vivo.
analysis.methods: They compiled 386 candidate genes from a protein interactome study and meta-analysis, narrowed the list to 290 after excluding essential genes, conducted an siRNA-based functional screen in influenza A virus-infected mouse L929 cells, and generated 84 knockout mouse lines.
analysis.main_results: After challenging the 84 mouse lines with a lethal dose of the mouse-adapted pandemic influenza A(H1N1) strain MA-CA04, they identified 17 gene-modified lines with increased resistance to infection, with Arhgef28- and Lasp1-modified mice showing robust protection in both sexes.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Although the molecular mechanisms remain unclear, these findings provide a valuable resource of validated host targets for future antiviral therapeutic development and reveal sex-specific effects not apparent in cell culture studies.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The identified host factors could inform the development of novel antiviral therapies and highlight the importance of considering sex-specific responses in influenza research.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's evidence strength is moderate due to the use of a single mouse-adapted strain and the unclear molecular mechanisms, though the large-scale in vivo screening approach provides robust data.

analysis.summary_en: This study addresses the limitation of in vitro studies by generating a library of CRISPR-Cas9-engineered knockout mice to identify host genes influencing influenza A virus susceptibility in vivo. The researchers screened 84 mouse lines with a lethal dose of the mouse-adapted pandemic influenza A(H1N1) strain MA-CA04, identifying 17 gene-modified lines with increased resistance. Notably, Arhgef28- and Lasp1-modified mice showed robust protection in both sexes, while other factors exhibited sex-specific effects. These findings provide a valuable resource for antiviral therapeutic development, though the molecular mechanisms remain unclear. The study highlights the importance of in vivo models and sex-specific responses in influenza research.

analysis.summary_en: This study analyzed the pathogen spectrum, co-infection characteristics, and risk factors for severe pneumonia in 2,149 pediatric inpatients with community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) in Henan Province from June 2023 to June 2025. The co-infection rate was 31.07%, with rhinovirus-Mycoplasma pneumoniae being the most common combination. Independent risk factors for severe pneumonia were underlying medical conditions (OR = 4.031) and a history of preterm birth (OR = 3.544). The findings highlight the importance of considering these risk factors in clinical management and surveillance of CAP in children.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Early diagnosis of Influenza A virus is critical for influenza prevention and control by reducing severe illness and mortality.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study developed a luminescence quenching lateral flow immunoassay (LFIA) platform for H1N1 detection using upconversion nanoparticles, defect-engineered Cu3−xP, and dual aptamers.
analysis.methods: The platform integrates upconversion nanoparticles, defect-engineered Cu3−xP, and dual aptamers to achieve luminescence quenching via Förster Resonance Energy Transfer, with molecular docking verifying aptamer binding sites.
analysis.main_results: The tri-modal analytical platform achieves a limit of detection of 0.907 ng/mL for H1N1 hemagglutinin, with high sensitivity toward H1N1 over H7N9, H9N2, H6N1, H7N7, and H5N1.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret the synergy of luminescence, colorimetry, and photothermal signals as a scalable point-of-care influenza detection strategy optimizing LFIA for on-site viral diagnostics.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: This work provides a sensitive and specific point-of-care detection strategy for influenza, improving on-site viral diagnostics and potentially reducing severe illness and mortality through early diagnosis.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence strength is high as the study presents a novel tri-modal platform with a low limit of detection and validated specificity, though abstract-only evidence limits assessment of real-world applicability.

analysis.summary_en: This study addresses the critical need for early diagnosis of Influenza A virus by developing a high-efficiency luminescence quenching lateral flow immunoassay (LFIA) platform. The platform integrates upconversion nanoparticles, defect-engineered Cu3−xP, and dual aptamers to achieve a synergistic mechanism, resulting in a tri-modal analytical system with a limit of detection of 0.907 ng/mL for H1N1 hemagglutinin. The approach demonstrates high sensitivity toward H1N1 over other influenza strains and good anti-interference ability, providing a scalable point-of-care strategy for on-site viral diagnostics that balances sensitivity and specificity.

analysis.scope_and_question: The review examines human seasonal influenza B virus (FLUBV) with a focus on CD8+ T cell responses to conserved epitopes, contrasting with influenza A virus (FLUAV) and addressing the central question of how these responses could inform future vaccines and therapeutics.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review synthesizes current knowledge on FLUBV-derived CD8+ T cell epitopes at cellular and molecular levels, explicitly comparing FLUBV to FLUAV, and highlights the limited data available on FLUBV despite its role in human influenza infections.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The review concludes that CD8+ T cells recognize more conserved viral epitopes than humoral responses, offering potential for broader protection, but notes that FLUBV-specific CD8+ T cell epitope data remain sparse compared to FLUAV.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review identifies a significant knowledge gap regarding FLUBV-derived CD8+ T cell epitopes, spanning both immunological and molecular insights, and emphasizes the lack of comparative data between FLUBV and FLUAV in this context.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The review prioritizes research to characterize FLUBV-derived CD8+ T cell epitopes and their presentation by HLA class I molecules, aiming to guide the development of vaccines and therapeutics that leverage conserved T cell responses.

analysis.summary_en: This review addresses human seasonal influenza B virus (FLUBV) with a focus on CD8+ T cell responses to conserved epitopes, contrasting with influenza A virus (FLUAV). It highlights that current vaccines, which induce humoral responses against rapidly mutating surface glycoproteins, require annual updates, whereas CD8+ T cells target more conserved epitopes, offering potential for broader protection. The review synthesizes existing knowledge on FLUBV-derived CD8+ T cell epitopes at cellular and molecular levels, explicitly comparing FLUBV to FLUAV. It concludes that CD8+ T cell responses to FLUBV are understudied, with limited data available despite FLUBV's significant role in human influenza infections. The review identifies a critical gap in understanding FLUBV-specific CD8+ T cell epitopes and their HLA class I presentation, emphasizing the need for further research to inform the development of vaccines and therapeutics leveraging conserved T cell responses.

analysis.research_question_and_background: England experienced an unusually early and rapid increase in influenza A/H3N2 subclade K infections during the 2025/26 season, raising concerns over a potentially severe epidemic due to antigenic change and a fast selective sweep.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study compared epidemic dynamics of the 2025/26 influenza A/H3N2 season to previous years using routine surveillance data in England, and developed an age-stratified transmission model and interactive web tool to explore scenarios.
analysis.methods: Peak epidemic growth rates and reproduction numbers were estimated using a Gaussian random walk model and EpiEstim, respectively, while scenario analyses varied immune escape, transmissibility, and seed date using 2022/23 as a baseline season.
analysis.main_results: Peak A/H3N2 growth rates and time-varying reproduction numbers for the 2025/26 season were of similar magnitude but occurred earlier than in previous severe seasons.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The 2025/26 season is characterised by early but not unusually rapid growth, and earlier growth does not systematically lead to especially large epidemics due to earlier susceptible depletion and a dampening effect from school holidays.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings support the need for complementary real-time epidemiological analyses and modelling alongside laboratory evidence for antibody escape to inform public health responses.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study cannot distinguish the relative importance of immune escape, increased transmissibility, or earlier seeding from the available data, limiting causal inference and highlighting moderate evidence strength.

analysis.summary_en: This mathematical modelling study assessed the 2025/26 influenza A/H3N2 season in England, which exhibited an unusually early increase in cases linked to antigenic change and a fast selective sweep. Using routine surveillance data, the authors compared epidemic growth rates and reproduction numbers across seasons from 2011/12 to 2025/26, estimating peak growth with Gaussian random walk models and EpiEstim. An age-stratified transmission model explored scenarios of immune escape, transmissibility, and seed date. The 2025/26 season showed early but not unusually rapid growth, with earlier trends compatible with moderate immune escape, a 10% higher R0, or an earlier seed date. The authors conclude that earlier growth does not necessarily result in larger epidemics due to earlier susceptible depletion and school holiday effects. The study underscores the importance of real-time epidemiological analyses alongside laboratory data to guide public health responses.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to explore the mechanisms linking depression and influenza A virus (IAV) infection and identify potential therapeutic targets. The background highlights that depression is associated with increased susceptibility to influenza, but the underlying mechanisms are unclear.
analysis.study_design_and_population: An integrated bioinformatics analysis was conducted using Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) datasets related to IAV infection and depression. The study focused on human subjects with depression and IAV infection, analyzing differential expression genes (DEGs) and immune-related pathways.
analysis.methods: The methods included differential expression gene (DEG) analysis, protein–protein interaction (PPI) analysis, Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analysis, immune infiltration and correlation analyses, single-cell RNA (scRNA) sequencing, virtual knockout (KO) simulation, molecular docking, and molecular dynamics simulations. In vitro experiments using IAV-infected Jurkat T cells were also performed.
analysis.main_results: 24 overlapping DEGs and 13 hub genes were identified through DEG analysis. PPI, GO, and KEGG enrichment analyses revealed these genes were mainly enriched in immune and inflammatory pathways. scRNA-seq analysis showed that IAV infection reduced CD4+ and CD8+ T cells infiltration while increasing macrophage-like monocytes abundance and significantly downregulating IL7R expression, especially in CD4+ T cells.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that IL7R may serve as a potential therapeutic target, and sanguinarine could be a promising candidate for treating depression combined with IAV infection through immune modulation. This is a novel finding as it links IL7R expression and immune cell dynamics to IAV infection in patients with depression.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that targeting IL7R could offer a new strategy for treating depression-related influenza susceptibility, potentially improving immune modulation and reducing viral replication in affected individuals.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study relies on bioinformatics analysis and in vitro experiments, which may limit generalizability to clinical settings. The evidence is moderate as it is based on computational methods and laboratory validation without direct clinical trials.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the link between depression and influenza A virus (IAV) infection through an integrated bioinformatics approach. It identifies 24 overlapping differential expression genes (DEGs) and 13 hub genes associated with immune and inflammatory pathways. IL7R is highlighted as a key gene, showing positive correlation with T-cell subsets and negative correlation with macrophages. scRNA-seq analysis reveals IAV infection reduces T-cell infiltration and downregulates IL7R, particularly in CD4+ T cells. Virtual knockout and molecular docking simulations suggest sanguinarine could modulate IL7R to reduce viral replication. The study proposes IL7R as a potential therapeutic target for depression-related IAV susceptibility, though the evidence is moderate due to reliance on computational and in vitro methods.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to describe the epidemiological pattern, temporal trends, and determinants of severe acute respiratory infection (SARI)-confirmed positivity for influenza and SARS-CoV-2 among hospitalized patients in Cambodia from 2020 to 2024.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A hospital-based retrospective cross-sectional surveillance data analysis was conducted using national sentinel SARI surveillance data collected from 2020 to 2024 across nine SARI sentinel hospitals in Cambodia, involving a total of 16,739 hospitalized patients who met the SARI case definition.
analysis.methods: Descriptive and bivariate analyses were performed, followed by multivariate logistic regression to identify factors associated with SARI-confirmed positivity, which was defined as laboratory-confirmed influenza or SARS-CoV-2 infections.
analysis.main_results: Among 16,739 SARI cases, 13.5% were laboratory-confirmed for influenza or SARS-CoV-2. A(H3N2) dominated in 2020, followed by widespread SARS-CoV-2 circulation in 2021. In 2022, SARS-CoV-2 co-circulated with A(H3N2) and influenza B (Victoria). In 2023, A(H1N1)pdm became the predominant strain as SARS-CoV-2 and A(H3N2) declined. In 2024, A(H3N2) again led circulation, with B(Victoria) and SARS-CoV-2 also detected. Sporadic A(H5N1) cases began appearing in late 2023.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings highlight the changing influenza subtypes circulating each year and the impact of the Delta variant of SARS-CoV-2 on SARI trends in Cambodia, with age, region, year, and season identified as significant factors associated with SARI-confirmed positivity.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results provide insights into the epidemiological dynamics of seasonal influenza viruses in Cambodia, emphasizing the need for targeted interventions and preventive measures for high-risk groups during specific seasons and regions.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective design and reliance on surveillance data, which may introduce bias and affect the generalisability of findings. The evidence is moderate in strength due to these limitations.

analysis.summary_en: This study analyzed the epidemiology of influenza and SARS-CoV-2 among severe acute respiratory infection (SARI) patients in Cambodia from 2020 to 2024. It aimed to understand the trends and determinants of SARI-confirmed positivity. The study used data from nine sentinel hospitals and found that 13.5% of SARI cases were laboratory-confirmed for influenza or SARS-CoV-2. A(H3N2) was dominant in 2020, followed by SARS-CoV-2 in 2021, and A(H1N1)pdm09 in 2023. In 2024, A(H3N2) reemerged, with B(Victoria) and SARS-CoV-2 also detected. The study identified age, region, year, and season as significant factors associated with SARI-confirmed positivity. The findings suggest the need for targeted interventions for high-risk groups. The evidence is moderate due to the retrospective design and potential biases in surveillance data.

analysis.methods: Through nasopharyngeal samples and questionnaires, we investigated risk factors including exposure periods and usage of personal protective equipment (PPE), and characteristics of influenza A(H5N1) infection.

analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform the need for continued PPE use and enhanced surveillance to monitor and mitigate the risk of animal-human transmission of influenza A(H5N1).
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on self-reported PPE use and the small number of PCR-positive cases, which may affect the strength of the evidence. The evidence is moderate in strength.

analysis.summary_en: This cohort study investigated the risk of human infection from exposure to highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) in England between 2023 and 2025. The study recruited 428 individuals at 34 outbreak sites and used nasopharyngeal samples and questionnaires to assess risk factors such as PPE use and vaccination status. Six individuals tested PCR-positive for A(H5N1), with three meeting the case definition for infection. No severe illness or secondary cases were reported. None of the cases were vaccinated against seasonal influenza, and two individuals did not use full PPE. The authors concluded that continued PPE use and enhanced surveillance are necessary to mitigate pandemic risk. The study's findings are of moderate evidence strength due to the small number of cases and reliance on self-reported data.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Understanding the sources of genetic diversity in Influenza A Virus (IAV) infections is crucial for understanding the mechanisms of viral evolution and immune escape.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Prior studies have characterized the effects of population bottlenecks during host-to-host transmission and intrahost tissue-to-tissue dissemination, but the role of intracellular replication processes on IAV genetic diversity remains largely unexplored.
analysis.methods: In this study, stochastic mathematical modeling was used to simulate the replication of genetically distinct IAV strains within individual cells and tissues.
analysis.main_results: Our results reveal significant bottleneck effects within a single infection cycle of individual cells.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Intracellular bottleneck effects are driven by stochastic molecular processes and lead to the expansion or elimination of neutral variants, creating large-scale differences between the initial and final frequencies of genetic variants in individual cells.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: By expanding our findings to a population-level model, we show that IAV intracellular replication reduces the effective population size, thereby diminishing the impact of selection and increasing the role of genetic drift.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: Our findings highlight the impact of intracellular replication processes on IAV genetic diversity, but the supplied evidence does not report specific limitations or evidence strength assessment.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the role of intracellular replication processes in shaping genetic diversity of Influenza A Virus (IAV). Using stochastic mathematical modeling, the researchers simulate the replication of genetically distinct IAV strains within individual cells and tissues. Their results reveal significant bottleneck effects within a single infection cycle, driven by stochastic molecular processes that lead to the expansion or elimination of neutral variants. The study demonstrates that intracellular replication reduces the effective population size, diminishing the impact of selection and increasing genetic drift at the population level. These findings provide insights into the mechanisms of viral evolution and immune escape, emphasizing the importance of intracellular dynamics in IAV genetic diversity. However, the evidence does not explicitly report limitations or the strength of the findings.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Avian-origin influenza A/H7N9 vaccines are poorly immunogenic in humans, and the cellular mechanisms by which oil-in-water emulsion adjuvants such as AS03 enhance immune responses remain incompletely characterized.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study enrolled 30 healthy adults and used RNA sequencing and quantitative proteomics to profile responses to two doses of an AS03-adjuvanted A/H7N9 vaccine across six immune cell types, comparing these responses to those elicited by an unadjuvanted seasonal A/H3N2 vaccine.
analysis.methods: Transcriptomic and proteomic profiling were performed to identify immune signatures unique to the AS03-adjuvanted vaccine and to correlate these signatures with subsequent antibody responses.
analysis.main_results: AS03-adjuvanted vaccination upregulated immune pathways in innate immune cells within 24 hours, including phagocytosis, antigen presentation and processing, inflammasome activation, NK-cell mediated cytotoxicity, IgA production, and interferon-response pathways.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings provide a mechanistic framework for how AS03 enhances vaccine immunogenicity, highlighting the role of neutrophils in MHCII-mediated antigen presentation as a previously underappreciated component of adjuvanted vaccine responses.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results inform pandemic influenza preparedness by identifying early transcriptomic and proteomic signatures that may guide the development and evaluation of adjuvanted vaccines against emerging influenza strains.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its small sample size and the absence of a non-adjuvanted A/H7N9 comparator arm, which constrains generalizability and the strength of causal inference; the evidence is assessed as moderate.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated why AS03-adjuvanted A/H7N9 vaccines are more immunogenic than unadjuvanted formulations by profiling early transcriptomic and proteomic responses in six immune cell types among 30 healthy adults. Using RNA sequencing and quantitative proteomics, the authors found that AS03-adjuvanted vaccination rapidly upregulated pathways involved in phagocytosis, antigen presentation, inflammasome activation, NK-cell cytotoxicity, IgA production, and interferon responses within 24 hours. Notably, MHCII gene transcription increased in neutrophils, suggesting a previously unrecognized role for these cells in antigen presentation. The findings provide mechanistic insights into how AS03 enhances vaccine-induced immunity and may inform the design of adjuvanted vaccines for pandemic preparedness.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addressed why the influenza B/Yamagata lineage appeared to go globally extinct after the COVID-19 pandemic while the B/Victoria lineage reemerged. It sought to determine whether epidemiological or immunological factors were primarily responsible for the extinction of B/Yamagata.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The authors developed a global mechanistic transmission model for the two influenza B lineages (B/Victoria and B/Yamagata) to simulate their dynamics before and after the COVID-19 pandemic.
analysis.methods: A global model was constructed to simulate influenza B transmission dynamics, incorporating a transient reduction in contacts to mimic pandemic impacts. Parameter values were identified to recapitulate pre-pandemic coexistence and post-pandemic outcomes for both lineages.
analysis.main_results: The model indicated that B/Yamagata’s extinction was primarily driven by its lower basic reproduction number, making it particularly vulnerable during the early pandemic phase. Stochastic simulations suggested B/Victoria was also close to extinction during this period.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors concluded that differences in intrinsic transmissibility, rather than cross-immunity or immune escape, best explained B/Yamagata’s extinction. They highlighted that their analysis uniquely combined mechanistic modeling with worldwide surveillance data to test competing hypotheses.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform influenza eradication strategies and biosafety policies by demonstrating that B/Yamagata’s extinction was likely due to its lower transmissibility, while also showing that B/Victoria narrowly avoided extinction and could sustain transmission if reintroduced.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study relies on a modeling framework and does not include empirical immunological or evolutionary data, which limits direct confirmation of mechanisms. The evidence strength is moderate due to the absence of experimental validation and reliance on surveillance data.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the apparent global extinction of the influenza B/Yamagata lineage after the COVID-19 pandemic, contrasting it with the reemergence of B/Victoria. Using a global mechanistic transmission model, the authors simulated pre- and post-pandemic dynamics by incorporating a transient reduction in contacts. Their results indicated that B/Yamagata’s extinction was primarily driven by its lower basic reproduction number, making it vulnerable during pandemic disruptions, while B/Victoria narrowly avoided extinction. The analysis ruled out cross-immunity or immune escape as primary explanations. The findings suggest that intrinsic transmissibility differences explain the observed outcomes and inform influenza eradication and biosafety policies, particularly regarding the potential for B/Yamagata’s reintroduction.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addressed the public-health need to monitor seasonal influenza viruses for reduced susceptibility to antiviral drugs during the high-severity 2024–25 season, when circulation of resistant variants could undermine treatment effectiveness. It aimed to quantify antiviral resistance markers and assess their impact on drug susceptibility and viral fitness.
analysis.study_design_and_population: CDC and public-health partners sequenced and analyzed genomes of more than 10,000 influenza viruses collected during the 2024–25 US influenza season. Sequence-flagged and representative viruses were tested in vitro for antiviral susceptibility.
analysis.methods: Whole-genome sequencing identified antiviral resistance markers, and phenotypic assays measured drug susceptibility of circulating viruses. CDC’s laboratory performed phenotypic testing to confirm sequence-based predictions and to identify new molecular markers of resistance.
analysis.main_results: Oseltamivir-resistant A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses with NA-H275Y were detected in 15 states at a low frequency of 0.53%. Influenza polymerase acidic (PA) mutations conferring 4- to 92-fold decreased baloxavir susceptibility were detected in nine influenza A viruses, and PA-I38T showed mild attenuation of replicative fitness in three cell lines.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the low but persistent circulation of NA-H275Y and PA-I38T viruses as evidence of human-to-human transmission despite no reported antiviral exposure in most patients. They highlighted the utility of whole-genome sequencing for surveillance and the necessity of phenotypic confirmation to validate sequence-based resistance predictions.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings inform antiviral stewardship by documenting the prevalence and fitness of drug-resistant seasonal influenza viruses, guiding recommendations on antiviral use and supporting the expansion of sequencing-based surveillance capacity in public-health laboratories.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study’s strength is bolstered by large-scale sequencing and phenotypic confirmation, but reliance on CDC laboratory for phenotypic testing limits throughput and generalizability. The evidence is moderate due to the absence of detailed clinical exposure data and potential under-detection of resistance outside sentinel sites.

analysis.summary_en: During the 2024–25 US influenza season, CDC and partners sequenced over 10,000 viruses and tested representative isolates for antiviral susceptibility. Oseltamivir-resistant A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses carrying NA-H275Y were detected in 15 states at a low frequency of 0.53%, while baloxavir-resistant viruses with PA mutations showed 4- to 92-fold reduced susceptibility and mild fitness attenuation in vitro. Most resistant viruses were collected from patients without reported antiviral exposure, suggesting onward human transmission. Whole-genome sequencing underpinned surveillance, but phenotypic confirmation remained centralized at CDC, constraining scalability. These data guide antiviral stewardship and underscore the value of integrating sequencing with phenotypic testing to monitor resistance in seasonal influenza.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Influenza A virus causes seasonal respiratory disease and its hemagglutinin (HA) protein undergoes continuous antigenic variation, driving pandemics. The study was needed because precise identification of B-cell epitopes within HA is essential for developing diagnostic tools and vaccine candidates to limit influenza spread.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study used an integrated experimental and bioinformatics strategy to design a trimeric HA protein, which was expressed in a mammalian eukaryotic system and purified by Ni-affinity chromatography. After animal immunization, nine HA-specific monoclonal antibodies were generated and characterized.
analysis.methods: B-cell epitopes on HA were mapped using the generated monoclonal antibodies through indirect enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), dot-blot, western blotting, and indirect immunofluorescence assays (IFA). The spatial distribution and structural characteristics of epitope regions were further analyzed using bioinformatics.
analysis.main_results: Six previously unreported linear B-cell epitopes were identified: 21GNDNSTATL29, 41IVKTITNDR49, 116YDVPDYASL124, 382DLKSTQAAI390, 458SEMNKLFEK466, and 488KCDNACIGS496. Bioinformatics analysis revealed their spatial distribution and structural characteristics on HA.

The novelty lies in the identification of six new linear B-cell epitopes on the HA protein.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings can inform the design of improved influenza subunit vaccines and diagnostic assays by targeting newly identified epitopes. They may enhance vaccine efficacy and enable more accurate detection of circulating influenza strains.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on in vitro epitope mapping and animal-derived monoclonal antibodies, which may not fully reflect human immune responses. analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to identify B-cell epitopes on the hemagglutinin (HA) protein of influenza A virus to support vaccine and diagnostic development. Using these antibodies, six previously unreported linear B-cell epitopes were mapped on HA through ELISA, dot-blot, western blotting, and IFA. Bioinformatics analysis further characterized the spatial and structural features of these epitopes. The findings expand the understanding of HA epitopes and provide a theoretical basis for developing subunit vaccines and sensitive detection methods. However, the study’s reliance on animal-derived antibodies and in vitro methods limits direct applicability to human immunity, warranting further validation in clinical contexts.

analysis.research_question_and_background: With the introduction of metagenomics in clinical diagnostics unfolding and the expanding role of pathogen genomics in national surveillance, conditions are favourable for the further maturation of these approaches in public health surveillance.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This prospective, pilot study included patients with acute respiratory illness attending GP practices participating in nationwide sentinel virological surveillance in the Netherlands, from Jan 10, 2025, to April 25, 2025.
analysis.methods: On predefined selection days, 90-100 combined nasopharyngeal and oropharyngeal swab specimens were analysed through parallel metagenomic testing using probes targeting 15 488 strains of human and animal viruses. Results were compared with a standard two-tiered surveillance strategy comprising PCR targeting 17 viruses, followed by amplicon-based nanopore whole-genome sequencing of influenza viruses, SARS-CoV-2, and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV).
analysis.main_results: 93 patients were included, with a median age of 51 years (IQR 33-67); 55 (59%) were women and 38 (41%) were men. Overall, 74 (80%) specimens tested positive through standard PCR-based screening.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Metagenomic surveillance detected viruses in 88 (95%) specimens, including DNA viruses known to establish latent infections. The data facilitated characterisation of a reassortant A(H3N2) influenza virus, potential vaccine escape mutants, markers of susceptibility to influenza antiviral drugs and RSV monoclonal antibodies, and a human A(H1N1)pdm09 influenza virus infection.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Further optimisation of probe-based enrichment strategies could reduce turnaround time and facilitate integration into routine public health surveillance.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: For viruses targeted by routine PCR, metagenomics showed a pooled sensitivity of 93·8% (95% CI 88·1-98·7), specificity of 99·8% (95% CI 99·5-100·0), positive predictive value of 96·2% (95% CI 91·8-100·0), and negative predictive value of 99·7% (95% CI 91·8-100·0), with a median genome coverage of 99·4% (IQR 96·9-99·9%). The technically robust and comprehensive performance across heterogeneous circulating viruses shown here supports evaluation in larger prospective studies in high-prevalence settings, where implementation might be most cost-efficient.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to pilot the use of probe-based metagenomics for nationwide sentinel surveillance of viral respiratory infections in primary care. The research focused on detecting and characterising both anticipated and emerging respiratory viruses, including seasonal influenza A(H1N1)pdm09, A(H3N2), and B/Victoria lineage. The study included 93 patients with acute respiratory illness in the Netherlands, from January 10 to April 25, 2025. Metagenomic testing identified viruses in 88% of specimens, including DNA viruses and influenza variants. The results demonstrated high sensitivity and specificity for targeted viruses, with comprehensive genomic characterisation. The findings suggest that probe-based metagenomics could be a valuable tool for public health surveillance, especially in high-prevalence settings. However, the study was limited to a pilot scale and requires further validation in larger studies.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Seasonal influenza continues to cause substantial morbidity and mortality worldwide. Identifying reliable clinical and paraclinical predictors of adverse outcomes may aid in early triage and management.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This retrospective study analyzed 294 RT-PCR-confirmed influenza cases admitted to Ayatollah Rouhani Hospital (Babol, Iran) during fall-winter 2022-2023. Key outcomes were prolonged hospital stay (> 5 days), ICU admission, and in-hospital death.
analysis.methods: Demographic, clinical, and laboratory data were extracted. Logistic regression and ROC analysis were used to identify independent predictors and cutoff values.
analysis.main_results: Prolonged hospitalization occurred in 43.5% of patients, ICU admission in 8.8%, and mortality in 5.0%. In multivariate analysis, opium use (OR: 5.4), renal disease (OR: 9.27), and LDH > 1000 (OR: 8.74) were significantly associated with longer hospital stay. LDH > 1000 also predicted ICU admission (OR: 46.9) and mortality (OR: 21.7). Oxygen saturation < 93% increased mortality risk (OR: 7.98). ROC analysis identified LDH ≥ 633 and CRP ≥ 88.5 as optimal cutoffs for predicting mortality.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Readily available markers such as LDH, CRP, liver enzymes, and oxygen saturation, which showed significant associations with prolonged hospitalization, ICU admission, or mortality in our analyses, may assist in early risk stratification of hospitalized influenza patients.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings may inform early risk stratification strategies for hospitalized influenza patients, potentially improving clinical decision-making and resource allocation.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is retrospective, which may introduce bias and limit the ability to establish causality. The evidence is moderate due to the observational nature of the study.

analysis.summary_en: This retrospective cohort study aimed to evaluate clinical and paraclinical factors associated with prolonged hospitalization, ICU admission, and in-hospital mortality in influenza-positive patients. The study analyzed 294 RT-PCR-confirmed influenza cases from Ayatollah Rouhani Hospital in Iran during fall-winter 2022-2023. Key outcomes included prolonged hospital stay (>5 days), ICU admission, and mortality. Logistic regression and ROC analysis were used to identify predictors and cutoff values. Results showed that opium use, renal disease, and LDH > 1000 were significantly associated with longer hospital stays, while LDH > 1000 also predicted ICU admission and mortality. Oxygen saturation < 93% increased mortality risk. ROC analysis identified LDH ≥ 633 and CRP ≥ 88.5 as optimal cutoffs for mortality prediction. The authors suggest that these markers may aid in early risk stratification of hospitalized influenza patients. The study's retrospective design limits confidence, and the evidence is considered moderate.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Influenza imposes a substantial global health burden, including increased risks of cardiovascular events beyond respiratory illness. However, regional data on influenza-associated excess mortality, particularly subtype-specific contributions and high-risk populations, remain insufficient in Guangxi, China.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This ecological time-series study collected weekly mortality data, influenza virological surveillance data for A/H3N2, A/H1N1, and B/Victoria, meteorological data, and air pollution data (PM2.5, NO2) from a city in Guangxi between the 14th week of 2022 and the 13th week of 2025.
analysis.methods: A generalized additive model (GAM) with a quasi-Poisson distribution was used to estimate influenza-associated excess mortality, adjusting for temperature, humidity, PM2.5, and NO2. The optimal lag structure was determined using QAIC-based model comparison, with excess mortality estimated via counterfactual predictions setting all influenza terms to zero. Negative binomial models were fitted as a sensitivity analysis.
analysis.main_results: The model explained 77.9% of deviance in all-cause mortality (adjusted R2 = 0.7275). The all-cause excess mortality rate was highest in 2023–2024 (42.36 per 100,000), followed by 2022–2023 (21.00 per 100,000) and 2024–2025 (15.57 per 100,000). Circulatory deaths constituted the majority of excess mortality, and the elderly (≥65 years) accounted for 3,002 excess deaths. A/H3N2 showed the strongest association with mortality (IRR = 1.0017, P = 0.002).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study highlights that influenza-associated excess mortality in Guangxi is predominantly circulatory, concentrated among the elderly, and most strongly linked to A/H3N2. This provides novel regional evidence on subtype-specific contributions and high-risk groups to inform targeted prevention strategies.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings support prioritizing A/H3N2-focused vaccination and enhanced circulatory disease monitoring in elderly populations in Guangxi. They also underscore the need for integrated surveillance incorporating meteorological and air pollution data to refine risk assessment.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The ecological design limits causal inference, and the study relies on aggregated data without individual-level clinical confirmation of influenza infection. The model's explanatory power is high for all-cause mortality, but subtype-specific estimates may be influenced by surveillance biases and unmeasured confounders, warranting cautious interpretation.

analysis.summary_en: This study quantified influenza-associated excess mortality in a city in Guangxi, China, from 2022 to 2025 using a generalized additive model adjusted for meteorological and air pollution factors. The model explained 77.9% of deviance in all-cause mortality, with the highest excess mortality rate in 2023–2024 (42.36 per 100,000). Circulatory deaths dominated excess mortality, and the elderly (≥65 years) accounted for 3,002 excess deaths. A/H3N2 showed the strongest association with mortality (IRR = 1.0017, P = 0.002). The findings highlight the predominance of circulatory disease in influenza-associated mortality, the concentration of risk in the elderly, and the dominant role of A/H3N2, providing regional evidence to guide targeted prevention and control strategies.

These results suggest a potential link between IAV infection and appendicitis, implicating immune responses in the disease's pathophysiology. However, the study's small sample size and use of correlation analysis without causation testing limit the confidence in its findings, resulting in moderate evidence strength.

analysis.methods: Pathogen screening was conducted using targeted next-generation sequencing (tNGS) to identify the presence of influenza A and B viruses. Multivariable logistic regression was performed to analyze independent predictors for respiratory support requirements.

analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform clinical vigilance for respiratory progression in pediatric IBV inpatients and highlight the importance of considering IBV as a significant pathogen in hospitalized children with acute respiratory infections.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its observational design and potential confounding factors, but the evidence is strong due to the use of targeted next-generation sequencing and multivariable logistic regression analysis.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to characterize the clinical and epidemiological features of hospitalized children with influenza B virus (IBV) and compare them with those of influenza A virus (IAV). The study highlights the need for vigilance in pediatric IBV inpatients and underscores the importance of IBV in clinical settings. However, the observational design and potential confounding factors limit the confidence in the findings, though the evidence is considered strong due to the robust analytical methods used.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Influenza A viruses, particularly H1N1 and H3N2, differ in their pathogenicity and host interactions, yet their impacts on gut microbiota and host metabolism remain poorly characterized.
analysis.study_design_and_population: In this study, we investigated the effects of H1N1 and H3N2 influenza virus subtypes on the gut microbiota and serum metabolites of Bama pigs through macrogenomic sequencing and untargeted metabolomics analyses.
analysis.methods: Both H1N1 and H3N2 infections significantly altered the gut microbiota composition and serum metabolite profiles, with H3N2 inducing more pronounced changes.
analysis.main_results: H3N2 infection markedly increased the relative abundance of Firmicutes, reduced Bacteroidota, and further depleted short-chain fatty acid-producing bacteria in the gut microbiota.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Serum metabolomic analysis revealed broader metabolic perturbations under H3N2 infection, including disruptions in glycolysis, amino acid metabolism, and related pathways.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Correlation analysis demonstrated significant associations between specific gut microbes and serum metabolites; for example, Prevotella was positively correlated with amino acid biosynthesis pathways.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: These findings indicate that influenza virus subtypes can remodel host metabolic states through gut microbiota-metabolite interactions, expanding current understanding of host responses to influenza infection and providing a data-driven foundation for future prevention and intervention strategies.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the effects of H1N1 and H3N2 influenza virus subtypes on the gut microbiota and serum metabolites of Bama miniature pigs. The research highlights that both subtypes alter gut microbiota composition and serum metabolite profiles, with H3N2 causing more pronounced changes. H3N2 infection was found to increase Firmicutes abundance, reduce Bacteroidota, and deplete short-chain fatty acid-producing bacteria. Serum metabolomic analysis showed broader metabolic disruptions, including impacts on glycolysis and amino acid metabolism. Correlation analysis revealed associations between gut microbes and serum metabolites, such as Prevotella with amino acid biosynthesis pathways. The findings suggest that influenza virus subtypes can influence host metabolic states via gut microbiota interactions, offering insights into host responses and potential strategies for prevention and intervention. However, the study is limited to animal models and does not include human data, which may affect the generalizability of the results.

The research underscores the importance of considering the type of NSAID used in influenza treatment, particularly in vaccinated and unvaccinated patients. The findings may guide clinical practice in managing influenza-related complications. However, the study's retrospective design limits confidence in its conclusions, and the evidence is considered moderate in strength.

analysis.summary_en: This study analyzed routine surveillance data from a rural health zone in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) during 2024–2025 to investigate co-circulation and co-infection of SARS-CoV-2 and influenza following a health alert for increased acute respiratory infection (ARI) cases and deaths. The authors emphasize the need to strengthen routine surveillance to better understand co-circulation patterns and clinical impacts in DRC. However, the small sample size (2% of suspected cases) and absence of detailed clinical outcomes limit the generalizability and robustness of the findings.

analysis.scope_and_question: The study examines the incidence and outcomes of acute respiratory deterioration fulfilling acute exacerbation (AE) criteria in hospitalized patients with pre-existing interstitial lung disease (ILD) after laboratory-confirmed seasonal influenza infection, focusing on the clinical burden and prognosis of such events in this vulnerable population.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review is a single-center retrospective cohort study of adults with pre-existing ILD hospitalized with influenza at Toranomon Hospital between April 2014 and April 2019. Influenza was confirmed by rapid diagnostic tests, and AE-criteria fulfillment was adjudicated by two pulmonologists and one radiologist. Baseline characteristics and outcomes were compared using the Mann–Whitney U test, Fisher’s exact test, Kaplan–Meier method, and log-rank test.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Acute respiratory deterioration fulfilling AE criteria occurred in approximately one fifth (21.3%) of hospitalized patients with ILD after laboratory-confirmed influenza. Patients with AE-criteria events had significantly lower percent predicted forced vital capacity (70.0% vs. 88.0%, p = 0.041) and higher ILD-GAP stage compared to those without such events. The in-hospital mortality rate in patients with AE-criteria events was 30.0%, and overall survival from influenza diagnosis appeared shorter in unadjusted analysis.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The study findings are exploratory and hypothesis-generating, requiring confirmation in larger multicenter studies. The unadjusted survival analysis limits causal inference, and the reliance on rapid diagnostic tests for influenza confirmation may introduce misclassification bias. The absence of multivariable adjustment for confounding factors further constrains the robustness of the observed associations.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Future research should prioritize multicenter prospective studies with multivariable adjustment to validate the observed associations and clarify mechanisms linking influenza to AE in ILD. Clinically, heightened surveillance and early intervention strategies for influenza in patients with ILD may be warranted given the high in-hospital mortality and shorter survival observed in those with AE-criteria events.

analysis.summary_en: This single-center retrospective cohort study evaluated the incidence and outcomes of acute respiratory deterioration fulfilling acute exacerbation (AE) criteria in hospitalized patients with pre-existing interstitial lung disease (ILD) after laboratory-confirmed seasonal influenza infection. Among 47 patients with ILD hospitalized with influenza, 21.3% developed AE-criteria events, which were associated with lower percent predicted forced vital capacity (70.0% vs. 88.0%, p = 0.041), higher ILD-GAP stage, and a 30.0% in-hospital mortality rate. Unadjusted analysis suggested shorter overall survival in these patients. The findings are exploratory and require confirmation in larger multicenter studies due to potential biases and unadjusted confounding.

analysis.summary_en: This prospective matched cohort study in Suzhou, China (2015–2018) assessed whether seasonal influenza during pregnancy affects fetal and infant health outcomes. Among 441 pregnant women with laboratory-confirmed influenza and 1,764 matched controls, maternal influenza was associated with a higher risk of late pregnancy loss (adjusted hazard ratio 31.1, 95% CI 1.3–756.8) but not early pregnancy loss. The authors conclude that influenza during pregnancy may increase risks to both pregnancy viability and early child health, aligning with vaccination recommendations.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Seasonal influenza vaccination shows highly variable effectiveness across individuals, particularly in older adults, in whom age-related immune decline compromises protective responses.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This study evaluated immune responses to the 2019/2020 quadrivalent influenza vaccine in 75 individuals aged 25–89 years. Participants were stratified as high or low responders based on influenza-specific antibody titers and virus-neutralizing activity measured before and four weeks after vaccination.
analysis.methods: Influenza-specific antibody titers and virus-neutralizing activity were measured before and four weeks after vaccination. Participants were stratified as high or low responders based on these measurements.
analysis.main_results: We observed that older individuals exhibited increased frequencies of myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) and activated regulatory T cells (Treg) expressing HLA-DR and CD38, consistent with enhanced immunosuppressive activity. Higher levels of these immunoregulatory populations correlated with poor vaccine responsiveness in both adult and older participants. Additionally, circulating T follicular regulatory (Tfr) cells were elevated in older participants and in low responders, whereas T follicular helper (Tfh) cells remained unchanged, resulting in an increased Tfr/Tfh ratio associated with impaired antibody production.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: These findings suggest that immunoregulatory networks, while essential for controlling chronic inflammation during aging, may limit vaccine-induced immunity.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Identifying biomarkers such as MDSC frequency, activated Treg phenotype, and Tfr/Tfh balance may contribute to the identification of individuals with different levels of vaccine responsiveness and could help inform future personalized vaccination strategies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: When adjusting for possible confounders, most immunoregulatory subsets did not remain independently associated with responder status, except CD38+ Treg cells.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated immune responses to the 2019/2020 quadrivalent influenza vaccine in individuals aged 25–89 years, focusing on the association between immunosuppressive cell populations and vaccine effectiveness. The research found that older adults had higher frequencies of myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) and activated regulatory T cells (Treg) expressing HLA-DR and CD38, which correlated with poor vaccine responsiveness. Additionally, an increased Tfr/Tfh ratio was observed in older participants and low responders, linked to impaired antibody production. However, after adjusting for confounders, only CD38+ Treg cells remained independently associated with responder status. The authors suggest that immunoregulatory networks may limit vaccine-induced immunity in older adults, highlighting potential biomarkers for personalized vaccination strategies. The study's findings contribute to understanding age-related immune decline and its impact on vaccine effectiveness, but the evidence is limited by the adjustment for confounders.

analysis.study_design_and_population: The study combined previous insights with structure prediction methods, molecular dynamics simulations, and experimental validation to define the human MxA L4 loop binding interface to THOV NP. It evaluated the stability of MxA L4-NP binding through classical all-atom molecular dynamics simulations.
analysis.methods: The study used structure prediction methods, molecular dynamics simulations, and a viral minireplicon assay to test predictions about MxA-THOV NP interactions. It also included evolutionary analysis and mutagenesis from earlier studies.
analysis.main_results: The model revealed MxA L4 binding to a surface-exposed site on THOV NP, including residues previously linked to viral escape from MxA restriction. The study predicted specific variants in human MxA or THOV NP that could result in increased host restriction or viral escape.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings provide a detailed understanding of the MxA-THOV NP interface, which is distinct from NP's RNA-binding or oligomerization surfaces. This information was not used to guide the modeling efforts, highlighting the novelty of the results.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results will guide vital viral surveillance studies and the development of MxA-based antivirals, offering insights into host-virus interactions that could inform future therapeutic strategies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is based on abstract-only evidence, and the findings are supported by molecular dynamics simulations and experimental validation, which provide moderate confidence in the conclusions.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the MxA-Thogotovirus nucleoprotein interface that mediates restriction and escape. It combines structural modeling, molecular dynamics simulations, and experimental validation to define the binding site on THOV NP. The results show that MxA L4 binds to a surface-exposed region of THOV NP, including residues associated with viral escape. The findings suggest that this interface is distinct from RNA-binding or oligomerization sites on NP. The study's results have implications for viral surveillance and the development of MxA-based antivirals. However, the evidence is based on abstract-only data, and the conclusions are supported by moderate confidence due to the reliance on simulations and experimental validation.

Phylogenetic analysis revealed multiple reassortment events between C.3 and C.5 clades and independent acquisitions of the D197N mutation, which restores a glycan masking a key neutralizing epitope. Removal of the glycan at residue 197 restored antibody recognition, demonstrating its critical role in antigenic drift. The 2025–26 and 2026 Southern Hemisphere vaccine strains are antigenically mismatched with C.3.1/re, and the 2026–27 Northern Hemisphere vaccine strain may also fail due to loss of the 197 glycan. These findings underscore the need for enhanced surveillance and adaptive vaccine strain selection to address the expanding antigenic diversity of IBV.

This systematic review aimed to identify determinants of SIV uptake among adults aged ≥50 years during and after the COVID-19 pandemic.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: We searched PubMed, MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, Global Health, CINAHL, Cochrane Library, APA PsycINFO, and APA PsycArticles for studies published between 1 December 2019 and 1 January 2026. The pooled prevalence of SIV uptake was synthesized using random-effects models in meta-analysis.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: A total of 50 studies were included in the systematic review. The pooled prevalence of SIV uptake among adults aged 50 years or above was 53% (95% confidence interval: 44–62%). Such uptake appeared lower among adults aged 50–64 years, in regions without a fully subsidized SIV, and after the COVID-19 pandemic.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: Subgroup analysis showed that cost and inaccessibility were barriers to receiving SIV in places without a fully subsidized SIV, and perceived susceptibility and vaccine safety concerns were commonly identified as facilitators and barriers in studies with data collected after the pandemic. More studies are needed to explore determinants specific to people aged 50–64 years to inform health promotion tailored to their needs.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: These findings could inform service planning and interventions promoting SIV uptake among adults aged ≥50 years in the post-pandemic era.

analysis.summary_en: This systematic review examines the determinants of seasonal influenza vaccination (SIV) uptake among adults aged ≥50 years during and after the COVID-19 pandemic.
